issues.title: Difference between "unknown" and "allowed"
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing WLGC issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3Awglc) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

_Raised in [email by EKR](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/dxpLCD7R2L-L07fEQCITjXjUcMY)_

S 3.

    After processing a statement of preferences the recipient associates
    each category of use one of three preference values: "allowed",
    "disallowed", or "unknown".  In the absence of a statement of
    preference, all usage categories are assigned a preference value of
    "unknown".

What's the semnatic difference between "unknown" and "allowed"?
Eventually, I need to either use or not use a given piece of
data. Is this just an internal detail of the algorithm?

### Proposed Resolution

_No response_

comments.author: mnot
mnot
comments.body: @ekr do still think this issue needs discussion?

comments.author: ekr
comments.body:
ISTM that there are two distinct questions:

1. Whether this document should take a position on default opt-in versus default opt-out, potentially driven by some background legal principles.
2. Whether this document should have an "unknown" state.

I'm skeptical of the background legal argument, as I doubt we're going to find that it's anywhere near that clear, but I don't think it's necessary to resolve the second question, to which I think the answer is "no".  What I mean specifically here is that the structure of this algorithm is that more specific preferences override less specific preferences (S 5.2). Thus, instead of carrying an unknown value all the way through the system, we should instead have the algorithm start with a default (possibly configurable based on local conditions) rule of allow or deny and then follow the rest of the algorithm as-is. The result is that any given category is always in a determinate state. This is a much more natural design and it's not clear to me we need anything fancier.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
The "defaults" question is #154. The only thing I'd point out is that text is non-normative; it's just signposting that we **don't** have an answer for this, so if someone wants a default they have to do it externally.

It sounds like you want to change that -- to require a default to be defined (and therefore part of the algorithm), even if that is done externally.

If that's the case a few things pop into mind:
- Preference hierarchy has turned out to be one of the contentious points in the group, so if we're going to take this approach, this has a dependency on eg #170
- Likewise, "top-level" / overarching preferences have also turned out to be contentious; we currently don't have one in the spec, meaning that this would be *required* to be defined eg by the legal regime, unless we come to consensus on a proposal there
- If that's the case, "unknown" is going to be a fact of life of this framework in operation (at least in places where the law doesn't define a default)
- We need to be certain that there is no semantic difference between a preference obtained through default vs one that's explicitly assigned
- It's not clear to me what the downside of having an unknown state is. Is this just a taste thing, or...?

comments.author: ekr
comments.body:
> It sounds like you want to change that -- to require a default to be defined (and therefore part of the algorithm), even if that is done externally.

Whether we write it down or not, at the end of the day the client has to either use or not use the content, and so unknown has to ultimately be lowered down to "allow" or "deny".


> Likewise, "top-level" / overarching preferences have also turned out to be contentious; we currently don't have one in the spec, meaning that this would be required to be defined eg by the legal regime, unless we come to consensus on a proposal there

No, I don't think so. There's already some implicit policy for how to handle "unknown". In the current algorithm it's handled at the very end of the day by this rather vague text "One approach for dealing with an "unknown" outcome is to assign a
 default value.  This document takes no position on what default might  be assigned." I'm simply saying that it would be better have the algorithm start with a default value and leave it up to the implementation how to set that value.

> It's not clear to me what the downside of having an unknown state is. Is this just a taste thing, or...?

It's not clear to me what the upside of having an unknown state is.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
> Whether we write it down or not, at the end of the day the client has to either use or not use the content, and so unknown has to ultimately be lowered down to "allow" or "deny".

Sure, but we've never pretended that we provide all of the information necessary to make that decision. Even putting the defaults issue aside, we shy away from imperatives like 'allow' and 'deny' because we are (per charter) focused on _preferences_, not instructions. Having an explicit 'unknown' state aligns with that.

> I'm simply saying that it would be better have the algorithm start with a default value and leave it up to the implementation how to set that value.
...
> It's not clear to me what the upside of having an unknown state is.

OK. It sounds like this is an editorial style / clarity issue, not a fundamental problem in the spec.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body:
> Sure, but we've never pretended that we provide all of the information necessary to make that decision. Even putting the defaults issue aside, we shy away from imperatives like 'allow' and 'deny' because we are (per charter) focused on preferences, not instructions. Having an explicit 'unknown' state aligns with that.

The text explicitly uses the terms "allowed" and "disallowed". These appear frequently. For instance:

~~~
   After processing a statement of preferences the recipient associates
   each category of use one of three preference values: "allowed",
   "disallowed", or "unknown".  In the absence of a statement of
   preference, all usage categories are assigned a preference value of
   "unknown".
~~~

> OK. It sounds like this is an editorial style / clarity issue, not a fundamental problem in the spec.

I don't agree. It's an issue in the algorithm described in the text.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I'm going to disagree with @ekr.  In many systems, the realm of possibilities in response to an answer of "IDK" will still be Boolean.  In which case, "allowed"/"disallowed" is going to be the only thing you want.  That might even be most systems.

But I can't accept that go/no-go is not the only thing that applies here.  Maybe for some uses, putting content into a human review process is going to be viable.  Obviously, that's not the sort of thing you want to have to run before running an algorithm, but you might be OK with it afterwards.  (Again, obviously not now, where no content has associated preferences.)

Leaving that aside, the composition of preferences means that you can't feed a default in as the starting position.  You'd need a wholly different approach for resolving conflicts between preferences[^1].  If "disallow" is stronger than "allow" then you can't start with "disallow".  The same applies if there is any sort of precedence between the outcomes.  Precedence is currently a fundamental part of the algorithm.  If your goal is to challenge that, then we can maybe be clearer about that.

[^1]: Conflicts at different layers of a hierarchy are another separable question. I'm talking about having two preferences that say different things, such as a header that says one thing and robots.txt saying another.  We can also solve THAT in a different way as well, but one thing at a time, I guess.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body:
A few points:

First, I think Martin's response suggests that this is not just an editorial/style issue, so we should tee this up for discussion at the interim.

Second, I'm not sure I follow what you mean about composition. I agree with you that precedence at the same level is baked into the algorithm, but what I'm effectively saying is that implementations should start with what's effectively a preference at the most general level. Thus, any directive in this document would override it, in accordance with  " Preferences about more specific categories override those of any more general category."

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
March interim: (re this and defaults issue)

MT: EKR is trying to 'refactor the code'; I'm struggling to identify the concrete reason to change here. What's proposed is reasonable but I'm not sure there's value in doing so. Not substantive. Prefer we defer this.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body: Well, that may be MT's opinion, but I don't agree it's not substantive. I'm willing to defer this, I guess.

issues.title: Defaults
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing WLGC issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3Awglc) and this issue is not present there.

### Issue Description

_Raised in [email by EKR](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/dxpLCD7R2L-L07fEQCITjXjUcMY)_

S 5.

    One approach for dealing with an "unknown" outcome is to assign a
    default value.  This document takes no position on what default might
    be assigned.

I don't think this makes any sense. The purpose of this document
is to allow the processing agent to understand the declaring
party's preferences, and we don't even require the agent
to respect them, so it's weird to talk about defaults in
that context.

### Proposed Resolution

_No response_

comments.author: mcerdancch-png
comments.body:
Regarding defaults, I suggest that the vocabulary should promote accessibility-friendly defaults, especially for people with cognitive and learning disabilities.

When no explicit preference is provided, the system should fall back to defaults that reduce cognitive load  e.g. clear/simple text, predictable navigation, and visual supports. This avoids situations where lack of preference leads to inaccessible or overwhelming outputs.

In my applied research (Decàleg per a l’atenció al públic amb TEA, Cerdan-Chiscano, 2023, Diputació de Barcelona & Aprenem Autisme), one of the key findings is that defaults matter: providing simple explanations, clear documents, and advance information is essential to avoid communication breakdown.

I therefore recommend that the draft explicitly states that defaults should favour accessibility and usability, with cognitive accessibility as a key dimension.

issues.title: Automated Processing is too broad
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing WLGC issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3Awglc) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

_Raised in [email by EKR](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/dxpLCD7R2L-L07fEQCITjXjUcMY)_

As I and others have noted, "automated processing" essentially
sweeps in any web crawler. In particular, as noted by Greg Lindahl,
parsing the document to find links is plainly "automated
processing", so you just can't really have a crawler without
"automated processing", which makes this whole category redundant
with forbidding crawling in the existing robots.txt framework.


### Proposed Resolution

_No response_

comments.author: TimidRobot
comments.body:
See also [[ai-control] AI Processing - a more focused top category?](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/YQA1sJUZncVXqKQS4Uw1zuePv1I/) (markdown formatting added for clarity):
> I wonder if replacing "Automated Processing" (`all`) with "AI Processing"
> (`all-ai`) would help to increase the accuracy of the vocabulary without
> hindering its effectiveness. I think this change might reduce the chance of
> unintended consequences while keeping the essential function.
>
> ## Current text:
>
>> ### 4.1. Automated Processing Category
>>
>> The act of using automated processing on one or more assets to analyze text
>> and data in order to generate information which includes but is not limited
>> to patterns, trends and correlations.
>>
>> The use of assets for automated processing encompasses all the subsequent
>> categories.
>
>
> ## Proposed text:
>
>> ### 4.1. AI Processing Category
>>
>> The act of using AI processing on one or more assets to analyze text and
>> data in order to generate information which includes but is not limited to
>> patterns, trends and correlations.
>
> The use of assets for AI processing encompasses all the subsequent
> categories.

comments.author: felixreda
comments.body: The proposal by @TimidRobot at least has the distinct advantage of bringing the overarching category within the scope of the Charter. As it stands, Automated Processing would cover a lot of uses that cannot be subsumed under "how content is collected and processed for Artificial Intelligence (AI) model development, deployment, and use". That said, it would make the issue of landing on a clear definition of AI more urgent.

comments.author: Jo-Levy
comments.body: The category described by 4.1, automated processing, is not only overly broad, it is also not applied consistently with the other categories, train-ai and train-genai. These categories do not describe what is done to the digital content -- the describe the end purpose for which the digital content is being used. They are expressing a preference for their content to be used (or not) to train ai or to be used (or not) to train genai. The preference could apply to content being used by humans to train AI by an algorithm or by a simply computer program.  By contrast,the " automated processing" category does not describe or limit itself to the purpose of the processing --it simply expresses a preference based on the means by which data is "processed".  It is not even limited to processing after the data has been collected from the website, which is inconsistent with the many discussions on limiting the vocabulary to usage of content.  The category should be removed.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
_Also from @chrisn in [email](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/2ZbEx73js_cTQT8mI1Wy6_0ZC_s):_

The scope, set out in the Abstract and Introduction, "a vocabulary of preferences regarding how automated systems process digital assets" seems overly broad. As a publisher the usage I'm most concerned about is processing in AI systems, and in particular generative AI. Introducing a scope for all automated systems risks unintended consequences for other uses that are unrelated to AI. So I suggest more clearly scoping the document to AI related usage.

Following from the above, the Automated Processing Category defined in Section 4.1 should either be revised (the original Text and Data Mining was preferable, because it's more specific) or removed entirely.

comments.author: paul2keller
comments.body: I think for the time being @TimidRobot proposal to rename the category is the best proposal that we have seen (for renaming the category, and getting away from the badly chosen "Automated processing". @martinthomson I would suggest that me merge this into the current draft.

comments.author: coopdanger
comments.body: @TimidRobot how would you define "the act of using AI processing"? At present the text is circular, it says AI processing is the act of using AI processing.

comments.author: Jo-Levy
TimidRobot
comments.body:
> [@TimidRobot](https://github.com/TimidRobot) how would you define "the act of using AI processing"? At present the text is circular, it says AI processing is the act of using AI processing.

@coopdange

"AI" is defined in [section 2](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-04.html#section-2). I believe the use of "processing" is standard. Additionally, I think the rest of the sentence adds some clarity. Also see:
- #151

Also, while the proposed definition might benefit from improvement, in this regard it is no worse than the original text.

comments.author: coopdanger
comments.body:
@Jo-Levy wrote:

> The most straigthforward language would be to remove "AI" and "processing" so it reads: "The act of using an asset in an AI-based system or to train or fine-tune an AI-based system."
> 
> This would be extremely difficult to comply with short of not using the asset at all and, therefore, may have many unintended consequences, but at least for a logical starting point for discussion, it is internally consistent.

I would make this even simpler and broader. I think the intent of this category is not meant to be limited to training and fine-tuning. Plus fine-tuning is not a defined term in the spec and is likely to be hard to define. Suggestion:

"The act of using an asset in an AI system."

comments.author: TimidRobot
comments.body:
## Mistakes are my own I have paraphrased @martinthomson a couple of times below. Please assume any fault is my own. ## Pros and cons of a top level category The following table is from a a whiteboard (Zurich meeting?). I think it is prudent to reproduce it here in this issue: | For top-level | Against top-level | | --- | --- | |
  • Valid to express demand
  • Known / unknown / rapid change
  • Complete vocabulary
  • Alignment w/ regulation
  • Suits opt-in / optional
  • Promotes market
  • Ease of use
  • Vocabulary portability
|
  • Unintended consequences
  • Inhibits innovation
  • Misalignment w/ regulation
  • Bleed into non-A.I.
  • Inconsistent understanding
  • Charter impact
  • Definitional impossibility
  • Learning sharp tools
| ## Robots: Automated crawling First, I think it's worth noting the scope of [1. Introduction - RFC 9309: Robots Exclusion Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html#name-introduction): > Crawlers are automated clients. Search engines, for instance, have crawlers to recursively traverse links for indexing as defined in [[RFC8288](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html#RFC8288)]. If we were going to keep this category, more or less as-is, it might be better to replace "Automated processing" with Automated clients". ## "Automated" is important, but insufficient @martinthomson clarified during IETF 124 Montreal, that the "Automated" in "Automated processing" was, perhaps, misunderstood. (I know that I was laboring under a misunderstanding.) "Automated" already excludes many of the concerns that have been raised by this category (negatively impacting pro-social behavior such as browser accessibility, translation, etc.). However, additional concerns remain (negatively impacting pro-social behavior such as archiving, research, etc.). This clarification does not resolve the concerns listed above or in: - #169 - #178 ## Blocking on thresholds During IETF 124 Montreal @martinthomson also put forward the idea of further limiting the top level category by describing its relationship with humans. I think this idea holds promise, but it also raises the issue of quantified thresholds in defining that relationship and the tension between "automation" and "inference". Until we better define how the entire vocabulary will (or won't) handle inference, we can't (we mustn't) define a top level category. ## Support current removal of category @mnot wrote in [[ai-control] Status of the Vocabulary Terms](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/AM7lHX2TqoWGS_E0ieP_jh1t6Ic/): > However, based upon discussion both in the room and on the mailing list, it's become clear that the AI Output and Automated Processing categories are still very contentious. The language for defining them is unlikely to be suitable for a call for consensus without a complete overhaul. > > As a result, the chairs believe that their presence in the editors' drafts has become a distraction from discussions that might lead us in more fruitful directions. So, we will be instructing the editors to remove them from the next set of drafts. This is not a declaration that there is consensus to omit them from the documents. We encourage participants to make proposals for language in these areas that they believe will be able to achieve consensus. I think this is a prudent decision because: 1. I don't think the top level category currently passes a cost/benefit analysis due to the costs defined above (and the linked issues) 2. I think the top level category has already been in conflict with categories previously in the draft and will continue to be problematic until we resolve how the entire vocabulary will (or won't) handle inference ## Worthwhile utility I hope that continued work will allow us to define a top level category in the future that has mitigated the most significant concerns while preserving its utility.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Closing as Automated Processing has been removed.

issues.title: Focus on purpose of use rather than time of ingestion
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing WLGC issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3Awglc) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

_Raised in [email by EKR](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/dxpLCD7R2L-L07fEQCITjXjUcMY)_

I don't think this taxonomy is really going in the right direction. I
have some critiques of the specific categories but, more broadly, I
think this is tied to specific technology choices in a way that's
unlikely to age well. I think instead it would be much more useful to
focus on the uses to which the data will be put (i.e., the output of the model),
as that's really the source of unhappiness about these systems.

Just so we're on the same page modern LLMs work (very approximately)
by training on an enormous corpus of data which sets the model weights
(I'm deliberately conflating pre-training and fine-tuning).  They are
then prompted with input and asked to create output based on that
input, as well as the output it's already generated (collectively the
context). As part of that process, some models can also collect new
data and use that as part of the context (RAG). In the context of web
crawling, then we have two ways for data to get into the system:

- In the training phase and stored in the model weights.
- In the generation phase as part of the context via RAG.

This is an important technical distinction, but it's not clear why it
matters from the perspective of the site. Consider an AI system which
collects the same corpus as is currently used for pre-training but
only trains on a small portion of it and then when it's asked to
generate content, uses some kind of "internal RAG" to suck in the
relevant documents and generate the output (this is a lot more like
human brains seem to work in my experience, because we just can't
remember much stuff). From the perspective of the site this is the
same: the system is using the site's content to generate new content,
but in the taxonomy of this draft, this isn't AI training or even
generative AI training because it doesn't impact the model
weights. Obviously I have no idea if this is a productive technical
direction, but neither do you, and conformance shouldn't hinge
on whether it turns out to be.

In my opinion a much more productive direction would be to focus on
the application to which this data is being put.  I don't have
anything like a complete story, but it seems to me that we have some
understanding of the categories at either end of the spectrum:

- Indexing (search): where you attempt to determine which
  piece of content the user wants and steer them towards it.

- Substitution: where the service generates something that
  is effectively a substitute good for the content.

I think these are useful conceptually because the first is the
traditional one that I think people have generally accepted as "good"
and the second is the one that seems to be of most concern. Obviously,
it's not as clear as that because even before generative AI search
systems were producing substitute goods (infoboxes, etc.), but I think
that's a feature of this analysis, because sites often didn't like
that and I think this kind of taxonomy captures that intuition without
worrying about whether the substitute good was generated via some
LLM, deterministic hand-written code, or something in between.

In between these two, we have some other applications. For instance:

- Summarization (think AI overviews) this is a partial substitute, but
  often it comes with a source link which can steer traffic to the
  site.

- Generating original content that isn't a direct substitute.  An
  example here might be code generation: the other day I asked an AI
  to help write me a scraper for the IETF agenda [0] and while I'm
  sure it was inspired by a lot of existing scraping scripts, it's not
  like it plagiarized one of them in total or somehow reduced the
  demand for them (this is a distinct question from whether it
  injected some verbatim code).

Again, I don't claim that these are the right dividing lines, but I
think that this kind of analysis does a better job of capturing what
is actually concerning to sites about AI. The challenge then becomes
how to turn these into relatively precise definitions. This is
probably harder than the current definitions, but I don't think
precision is a virtue if the definitions aren't actually a good fit to
the problem they are trying to solve (as they say, "for every complex
problem there is an answer that is clear, simple, and wrong").

### Proposed Resolution

_No response_

issues.title: 3.2 Respecting Preferences
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing WLGC issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3Awglc) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

Per thread on the list, there is still contention about the text in 3.2.


### Proposed Resolution

_Sourced from e-mail by [Alissa](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/5vUslBkhFk-na7geaO_XFaWqc0c)_

1. Getting rid of the normative MAY. I know this was discussed on the PR thread before the -03 was published. This whole section is in the realm of non-technical considerations and using a normative keyword muddies that.

2.  Significantly paring back the text starting from “Usage preferences can be ignored …” so that it provides less fodder for future debate about what was really intended here. I have a suggestion below that echoes back to Lila’s original note about historic, widespread use of certain tools. I nixed “free expression” from the list as it felt like the everything category, but I think including the other examples is helpfully illustrative.

> Parties might choose not to honor preferences they receive on the basis of express agreements they have with other parties, for legal compliance purposes, or for other reasons. Historically, entities engaged in automated processing of digital assets in support of safety, education, scholarship, research, preservation, interoperability, accessibility, and other priorities have needed to make such choices in response to existing preference signaling mechanisms, and affected parties have had to grapple with the consequences. The preference statements described in this specification are no different.

comments.author: mcerdancch-png
comments.body:
I would like to highlight the importance of explicitly including cognitive accessibility preferences within this section.

People with cognitive and learning disabilities often need preferences such as:
– simplified or plain language,
– anticipation of steps in a process,
– additional response time,
– support with visual aids (icons, pictograms, real images).

These preferences must be respected in the same way as security or privacy preferences, because they directly affect users’ ability to interact with AI systems.

As an example, my research with public administrations in Barcelona resulted in a set of practical communication guidelines (Decàleg per a l’atenció al públic amb TEA, Cerdan-Chiscano, 2023, Diputació de Barcelona & Aprenem Autisme, available at: [ResearchGate link](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/395700660_Decaleg_pautes_atencio_al_public_amb_TEA)
). These show how respecting such preferences significantly improves usability for autistic people and others with cognitive disabilities.

I recommend extending the vocabulary to allow explicit declaration of cognitive accessibility preferences, so that systems are required to respect them.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
_From @chrisn in [email](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/2ZbEx73js_cTQT8mI1Wy6_0ZC_s):_

The list of examples in Section 3.2 of cases where preferences could be ignored, should be removed. The preceding paragraph in this section makes clear the considerations where preferences could be ignored, and the specification should not attempt to define or identify specific examples. This should be left to policymakers, and it may vary by legal jurisdiction.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
See also:
  https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-zehta-aipref-exclusions-00.html

comments.author: BradSilver99
comments.body:
A suggested alternative - striving for neutrality and does not override. 

This specification provides a set of definitions for different categories of use, plus a system for associating simple preferences to each (allow, disallow, or no preference (see [Section 3](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-05.html#model)). The categories defined in this specification are intended to describe functional outcomes of content use, rather than specific technical implementations or system architectures.

This specification does not provide any enforcement mechanism for those preferences, and is agnostic as to conformance with it by parties during data processing.  Legal or contractual agreements, rules and frameworks are outside the scope of this specification.
Specifically, preferences do not themselves create rights or prohibitions, either in the positive or the negative. Other mechanisms—technical, legal, contractual, or otherwise—might determine the consequences of following or not following a stated preference. As stated in § 1, expressing preferences is without prejudice to and does not override applicable laws and agreements, including the applicability of exceptions and limitations to copyright.

As enforcement is out of scope for  this specification, it also does not determine the consequences of respecting or ignoring preferences, which could vary depending on factors outside the scope of this document, such as applicable legal or contractual rules.

issues.title: Removal of "bots" from Vocab Section 6.1
issues.author: Jo-Levy
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing WLGC issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3Awglc) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

See Jlevy comment from 9/14   re the ambiguity, confusion, and potential  inaccurate overlap with the term "bots" in Section 6.1  as used in other IETF WG documents/charters:  

 I have searched the entire thread archive, but do not see any discussion regarding the use of the term “bots.”   

The other terms in 6.1 describe how the data is used, e.g. to “train” or “search.” But the term “bots” suggests it is based on who is using the data, rather than what is being done to the data. For example, in the WebBotAuthN Working Group, the term “bots” is  used to refer to “non-browser clients.” By using the term “bots” in Section 6.1, it creates an inconsistent approach that will lead to confusion about the meaning of the preference. Some people may incorrectly believe that bots=n is a preference to disallow access by bots. Others may incorrectly believe bots=n is a preference to disallow all use by bots, regardless of whether that use is for or related to AI. 

This is especially important because the Vocab and Attach documents are not intended to be read together all the time.  The Vocab is intended to also be a standalone document. As I understand it, members of this group are liaising with other standards bodies to export the final language from this document to other bodies for their use independently, without the structure of the Attach document or robots.txt.  See, for example, Leonard’s recent email stating: <<This vocab is designed to be used in any scenario - online or offline, web or otherwise - where someone wishes to express a preference about the AI usage of an asset.>>   Earlier drafts also called for the Vocabulary to “standardize building blocks” that could be used regardless of the manner of attachment. 

When the categories and descriptions in the Vocab document are considered as standalone expressions, it is even more important that their scope and intent is clear.

Proposal: delete the top category and the accompanying “bots” descriptor in 6.1.  This removes the ambiguity and confusion, maintaining the focus on AI and moving the group more toward consensus.

 See also PKeller reply 9/14 agreeing that the term "clearly also problematic" and suggesting focusing first on the automated processing category (which makes sense).

### Proposed Resolution

_No response_

issues.title: Choice of terminology regarding "asset"
issues.author: Jo-Levy
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing WLGC issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3Awglc) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

The term "digital asset" is used throughout the Vocab document.  It is confusing and misleading.  A "digital asset" generally and commonly refers to cryptocurrency. The United States Internal Revenue Service (IRS) defines it as "any digital representation of value on a cryptographically secured, distributed ledger (blockchain) or similar technology."  See https://www.irs.gov/filing/digital-assets#description.  
 It's not a term used in robots.txt or the Attach documet which uses the term "content" and "content-usage." A preferable term would be "Digital Content."

### Proposed Resolution

Replace "digital asset" or "digital assets" with "digital content." Replace "asset" with "digital content." Replace "one or more assets" with "digital content." There are 23 instances of the term asset or assets throughout the document.  By using "digital content" there is also no new for a definition of the term "Digital Asset."

comments.author: lrosenthol
comments.body:
On the other hand, @Jo-Levy - standards such as C2PA and JPEG Trust both use the term "asset" or "media asset" to differentiate the entire entity/file from just the "content" - in that there exists other parts (e.g. metadata) of an "asset" beyond just the content.

See https://spec.c2pa.org/specifications/specifications/2.2/specs/C2PA_Specification.html#_assets_and_content and https://ds.jpeg.org/documents/jpegtrust/wg1n100972-105-REQ-Terms_and_definitions_for_JPEG_Trust_v2_0.pdf

comments.author: chrisn
comments.body: I agree with @lrosenthol, asset is a recognised term, so I see no need for change here. There's a clear definition in the Conventions and Definitions section of the draft.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:

comments.author: sposth
comments.body: “Content” is very broad and refers to the expressive or informational layer, not necessarily the concrete digital file or file instance. If the vocabulary refers to identifiable media files – images, text files, audio files, video files – then “asset” is the more accurate technical term, because it describes the file as a discrete digital object. In the media and metadata domain, “digital asset” has been used in this sense for many years, unrelated to cryptocurrency.

issues.author: Jo-Levy

issues.title: Add non-enforceability provision similar to what is in the Vocab document
issues.author: Jo-Levy
issues.body:
### Confirmation

### Issue Description

Both robots.txt and the Vocab document have language clarifying that the documents do not include enforcement mechanisms.  The Attach document is not. Propose adding  non-enforcement provision similar to Vocab document.

### Proposed Resolution

Suggest adding new Section with non-enforceability language: 
 Non-Enforceability.   This specification is not enforceable.  An entity that receives content usage preferences MAY choose whether or not to follow the preferences.  Many factors may be considered in determining whether to follow a preference, including but not limited to  how the usage corresponds to the usage categories where preferences have been expressed, the type of content, the identity and authority of the Declarant to assert a preference over the specified content, the applicable legal context, or other considerations such as free expression, safety, education, scholarship, research, preservation, interoperability, and accessibility.

issues.title: Distinguishing access and use
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing WLGC issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3Awglc) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

I'm going to quote @coopdanger here, because her formulation of the issue is pretty good.  I will follow up with a nit on the details, but that doesn't diminish the value of the feedback:

> This raises the question of whether the vocabulary is only meant to be used to express preferences about usage and not initial access regardless of the attachment mechanism. The very first sentence of the vocab doc uses the ambiguous term “processing” while most of the rest of the doc uses “usage.” If the intent is to define a vocabulary that only expresses preferences about an asset after the asset has been obtained (by whatever means), it needs an explicit scoping limitation to that effect. And then every attachment mechanism that gets defined in the IETF or elsewhere needs to reflect that.
>
> Making this distinction explicit might be a simple resolution to some of the concerns that have been raised about the automated processing category, because it would make clear that it’s unnecessary to resolve the question of whether crawling/accessing a site is itself considered automated processing. No preferences are being expressed about access, other than insofar as sites would expect crawlers not to crawl their site if the site wishes to disallow all the uses of interest to the crawler. It would not resolve the concerns about behavior habituation and misinterpretation, though.
>
> Even with this distinction made explicit, there would still be the possibility of basically nonsensical use cases, e.g.:
>
> ```http
> User-Agent: *
> Content-Usage: /foo bots=n
> ```
> 
> Like what is the point of allowing crawling/access but then disallowing all usage? Maybe there is a use case I’m missing.
>
> Note also that it may be entirely unrealistic to say that everywhere an attachment mechanism is specified, it has to preserve this distinction between access and usage. It’s not like we can constrain mechanisms that get defined elsewhere.
> 
> I’ve never really been convinced of the need for the top-level category, but if we are going to have one we need to be clear about when it applies, and clarifying that it only applies after an asset has been obtained might help mitigate concerns about its breadth.

### Proposed Resolution

There was some effort to make this distinction in editing, but it's clear that we need to be much clearer about it throughout.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
The very pedantic nit...

The example probably needs an `Allow: /foo` line.  RFC 9309 is not clear when it comes to delineating groups, particularly when it comes to extensions like this one.  That means that a group with no Allow or Disallow lines might be joined to the next group.  That is, this might be one or two groups:

```
User-Agent: *
Content-Usage: /foo bots=n
User-Agent: bar
Content-Usage: /foo bots=y
```

The more substantive point is with respect to this:

> Like what is the point of allowing crawling/access but then disallowing all usage? Maybe there is a use case I’m missing.

As we have discussed at some length, these are preferences and so crawled content that has an associated preference that it not be used for any purpose is still available for use in cases where there is a reason to ignore preferences.

> Note also that it may be entirely unrealistic to say that everywhere an attachment mechanism is specified, it has to preserve this distinction between access and usage. It’s not like we can constrain mechanisms that get defined elsewhere.

I don't think that this is unrealistic.  Getting the bits and using them are distinct actions.  Consider where the preferences are carried in an HTTP header.  It's not like the response isn't delivered and available, even if the preferences indicate that the reason for making the request goes against the stated preferences.  This distinction recognizes that there are still cases where the use motivates (or justifies) ignoring the preference.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: See also #158.

comments.author: lrosenthol
comments.body: I would say that preferences are for use and not for access.

issues.title: Attachment: Section 2 preservation of HTTP request header "MUST" is too strong
issues.author: bnewbold
issues.body:
I think this is a couple days late for the formal WGLC, but hope it is helpful to file this here as an issue ahead of the upcoming meeting. I can also take this to the list if prefered.

### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing WLGC issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3Awglc) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

Section 2 of the Attachment draft has a new section about retaining the `Content-Usage` header from requests, and re-using them on responses for the same content later:

> Servers MUST retain any preferences associated with a request if the content of that request is used to answer later requests. For example, the content of a PUT request that is used to answer subsequent GET requests. Note that servers that have not been updated to understand this field will not comply with this requirement.

I think having the server retain the preference metadata is a great idea, but making it a "MUST" for any server which implements usage preferences is too restrictive. I believe servers should be allowed (and encouraged) to include this metadata header even if they don't have the means to implement state persistence based on request headers. Servers might implement alternative or more ergonomic mechanisms for expressing preferences, for instance via an HTML form field, and that is fine.

### Proposed Resolution

Make it "MAY".

Overall I think this should be more of a recommendation or best practice. Given that I would defer to the editors in terms of how best to phrase things.

issues.title: Automated Processing category risks jeopardizing a safe and working internet
issues.author: kmadhavan-msft
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing WLGC issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3Awglc) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

The current definition of “automated processing” is broad and ambiguous, encompassing routine functions like exporting to PDF, printing, or viewing content in a browser. As noted by Greg in the working group, even basic link extraction could fall under this category, potentially rendering all crawlers—including non-AI ones—inoperable. 

We’re concerned this framing could unintentionally undermine essential Internet functions such as content moderation, spam filtering, and accessibility features. While we recognize these outcomes are not the intent, the risk remains that critical functionality may be impaired, user expectations misaligned, and implementers exposed to complaints—especially in regulated contexts. 

It’s also worth noting that existing mechanisms already allow publishers to signal bot access preferences. If there are concerns about their adoption or effectiveness, that may be a more productive area for discussion—one we haven’t yet seen raised in this group. 

### Proposed Resolution

Remove the automated processing category. We believe that the Automated Processing category is too broad and vague and will lead to a less safe and open  and open Internet in the long run.

issues.title: Hierarchical structure is problematic and introduces unnecessary complexity
issues.author: kmadhavan-msft
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing WLGC issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3Awglc) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

The hierarchical structure in vocab-03 -  placing categories like Automated Processing, Search, and AI Training in parent–child relationships - introduces complexity without real benefit. In practice, preferences can be expressed directly on each activity, so the hierarchy does not add clarity; instead it forces artificial nesting. Real-world processing often overlaps across categories, and the hierarchy has already led to a patchwork of overlapping or conflicting proposals. Because publishers simply want to state “allow” or “disallow” for specific uses or use multiple preferences, the extra layer of hierarchy is unnecessary and risks confusing both implementers and publishers. A flatter, modular vocabulary would make preferences easier to understand, more consistent to apply, and better aligned with real systems. 

### Proposed Resolution

Remove the heirarchical structure and replace with a flatter, modular structure that would make the preferences easier to understand, more consistent to apply, and better aligned with real systems.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
@kmadhavan-msft You mention creating a "flatter, modular structure" -- could you give some more detail? In particular, what should be done when there is a case that _is_ a subset of a larger term?

For example, let's imagine that we've agreed on a term for "(A) AI for the purpose of creating media about animals", and want to create a new term for "(B) AI for the purpose of creating pictures of kittens." 

A recipient of "A=no" "B=yes" needs to disambiguate these seemingly conflicting signals; AFAICT we have a few options:

1. Make B a subset of A -- i.e., B is more specific and therefore wins
2. Define B to override a preference for A when stated (functionally equivalent to 1?)
3. Define A to be overridden by a preference for B (requires B to be known about when A is created)
4. Don't allow this pattern of definitions / we aren't going to need it

It seems to me that if terms are to have precedence, that needs to be defined somewhere, with the most likely candidates being the definitions of the terms themselves. If that is the case, I'm wondering whether you're objecting to the capability itself (i.e., 4 above), or it's just the terminology which is causing a problem.

issues.title: Search should be removed and replaced with display-based preferences
issues.author: kmadhavan-msft
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing WLGC issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3Awglc) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

The term “Search” is well understood by webmasters, but using it without a clear definition may cause confusion rather than helping address publisher concerns about display-based approaches. Yet, many challenges arise when attempting to strike a durable definition: 

The line between search and AI is increasingly blurred, making it hard to separate them meaningfully in policy. 

Modern search relies on AI for functions like ranking and snippets, so a distinct “search” opt-out may not be practical. 

The current “search” category appears to regulate internal system behavior in ways that are hard to define or audit. 

Existing mechanisms like robots.txt and noindex already give site owners strong control, so adding a new “search” category could duplicate or conflict with these mechanisms. 

### Proposed Resolution

We have proposed alternate solution detailed here: [https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-madhavan-aipref-displaybasedpref-01](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-madhavan-aipref-displaybasedpref-01 )

_From @chrisn in [email](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/2ZbEx73js_cTQT8mI1Wy6_0ZC_s):_

Without a category that covers RAG and grounding usage, the vocabulary does not meet publisher needs. This need was raised at the outset of this work, in the IAB workshop in Washington DC in 2024, and included in the WG charter scope.

In addition to reducing web traffic to original content, such usage introduces the possibility of creating misleading or biased statements, an issue that impacts news publishers in particular, risking undermining their credibility. Research published by the BBC goes into this in more detail, demonstrating that AI-generated answers summarise and present content in a way that can introduce factual inaccuracies and biases that are not present in the original published content.

### Proposed Resolution

_No response_

I strongly believe that a post-training/RAG category can't be left to future work - it needs to be part of the baseline framework which this document is attempting to outline.  The need and the prevalence of this activity is too broad to ignore, as are linkages to search as well as training. comments.author: paul2keller
comments.body:
here is a proposal for a category that I have been working on based on some side conversations. This builds on the way `ai-input` is defined in the [RSL](https://rslstandard.org/rsl#_3-4-1-1-usage-vocabulary) and [Cloudflare](https://contentsignals.org) vocabularies (which cover RAG), but added an exclusion for assets that are directly provided by the end user of the system as a user rights safeguard:

> `AI-input` Retrieving assets as input into an AI-based system to generate outputs that are presented to clients of that system (retrieval augmented generation). This does not include assets that are provided as input by end users of the AI-based system either directly or by providing the location of the asset(s).

comments.author: lrosenthol
comments.body:
> This does not include assets that are provided as input by end users of the AI-based system either directly or by providing the location of the asset(s).

I have significant objections to this sentence.  Adobe's Creative customers have a strong desire to be able to have their asset's associated preferences work in applications when directly presented as well.  For that reason, Adobe's applications (and services) today actively respect the `cawg.ai_inference ` preference when present in a CAWG training & data mining assertion (https://cawg.io/training-and-data-mining/1.1/).  That functionality is important to our customers and needs to be permitted.

comments.author: cantechit
comments.body:
This category doesn't address RAG for the purposes of training use.    If I could suggest text similar to.. 

Retrieving assets as input into an AI-based system to generate outputs that are presented to clients of that system (retrieval augmented generation).  This does not include assets that are provided as input by end users of the AI-based system either directly or by providing the location of the asset(s).   **RAG or AI-Input used for the purposes of retraining, refining  or creation of a foundation model is excluded by this section**

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
> This does not include assets that are provided as input by end users of the AI-based system either directly or by providing the location of the asset(s).

I would suggest instead that explicit user direction might be a reason an application would choose to ignore a preference. "The source of this image prefers that it not be used as input to AI-based tools. If you choose to continue, you assume any legal liability. Should I continue anyway?"

comments.author: natehake
comments.body:
This category should logically start where the training category ends. In other words, it should cover use of assets by an AI model that has been trained. 

As one potential starting point (which I may refine later), we could say: 

> **AI-Inference**: The act of using an asset for inference by an AI model that can generate content in one or more modalities (text, image, audio, etc...). Inference means all use beyond the production or refinement of an AI model. 

With respect to user-provided assets and other concerns about overly broad use, I think two approaches would potentially work: 1) having two versions of this category (one for use by end users, one for use by automated systems); and/or 2) addressing concerns about overreach at the top level, as we have for other definitions.

comments.author: llemeurfr
comments.body:
Adding an AI Inference property to the vocabulary, as a counterpart to the AI Training property, has been widely discussed, but hasn't reached consensus because Inference encompasses many different uses. This proposal creates three inference-type properties that appear to cover most uses of an AI Model, excluding Search and Discovery capabilities, which are treated separately.

First, we'll have to define the user-facing software solution powered by an AI model. Let's call it **AI system** =  a software that exposes AI-related functionalities (i.e., an AI model) to end users.

The three proposed properties are:
### AI Grounding
The act, for an AI system, of automatically selecting one or more assets for use as input to a trained AI/ML model, as part of the operation of that system.

Use case: 
- A RAG solution (a user submits a prompt to an AI system. The system uses the prompt to fetch a set of documents from the web, processes them to augment the prompt with additional context, and submits the augmented prompt to the underlying AI Model. 

### AI Input
The act, for an AI system, of using one or more user-selected assets as input to an AI/ML model as part of the operation of that system.

Use cases: 
- A user is reading a document in a reading system where the TTS feature is powered by AI. He selects a voice and hits the play button. 
- A user submits a PDF document to a translation software powered by an AI model. He chooses a target language and requests a PDF document in return.
- A user submits a document containing complex wording to an AI System. He requests simplified wording that he can better understand.
- A user is reading an ebook in an AI-powered reading system. Because he left the book aside to some time, and the reading system tracks where he left, he requests a summary of the previous chapters.
- A user submits a personal image and a reference image to an AI System. He asks the software to generate a target image from the personal image, in the style of the reference image. 

### AI Remix
The act of using an asset in an AI system to generate an output generated from a combination of assets. 

Use case: 
- A user sends a request to an AI System, which responds with a remix of different documents, with no hyperlink to the source of each document.  
- A user has gathered a set of documents relative to a specific topic. He asks an AI System to process the directory containing these documents, then prompts it to provide precise answers to his questions. 

The first property deals with content fetched and processed by an AI system without user intervention. The second is similar, but users somehow take responsibility for the choice of content used as input to the AI System. The third property is about the output of an AI System, not its input. 

Technically speaking, I'm not certain that an AI Remix can be obtained with content that is not used for AI Grounding or AI Input. But I understand that one aspect of our work is to keep a distance from what is feasible today. 

Happy to discuss this proposal.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body:

For example, suppose that I have a system where I have pre-retrieved a large group of documents and stored them locally and then feed them to the AI system as part of servicing a query. issues.title: Search is too Broad
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

_From @chrisn in [email](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/2ZbEx73js_cTQT8mI1Wy6_0ZC_s):_

While I appreciate the effort that has gone into crafting this definition, as it stands it still allows all the generative AI usage that publishers find problematic. If adopted, publishers will be in the position of having to allow the Search Category, because they cannot realistically opt-out of traditional (i.e., non generative AI search).

Given that major search engines are rapidly integrating generative AI features, a generative AI response to a user query that includes links provided via RAG or grounding could be interpreted as "directs users to the location from which the assets were retrieved". The qualifying statements: "Only those parts of applications that direct users to the location of an asset are included in this category of use. This includes the use of titles or excerpts from assets that are used to help users select between multiple candidate options" don't address this concern. The same applies to "Parts of applications that do not direct users to the location of assets, such as summaries, are not covered by this category of use", because search engines that integrate generative AI do produce summaries.

### Proposed Resolution

_No response_

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
From Bradley Silver in [email](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/zaXD4Ah5ruMVIr1sbdwMVeYkOIk):

On search, I agree with the concerns Chris raised - but I also wonder whether this is something that can be better clarified in the drafting, versus there being actual disagreement about what that category is intended to cover or not, when it comes to the line between search results and "answers" with citations.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
Hey @chrisn - to clarify: I understand that you want to express a preference for 'traditional' search while expressing one against 'ai' search. 

If a search engine returned a results page that looks like traditional search and happens to use AI to generate it, would you still want to disapprove of it? Or is there some other aspect that it's important for you to express a preference for?

comments.author: chrisn
comments.body:
Here's a proposed change to the definition of Search category, which focuses its scope a bit:

The use of one or more assets to create a search index for the purpose of providing search results in the form of returning links to a website's contents. Use includes:
* Backend Processing: The internal processing of assets to perform indexing, ranking, and retrieval may utilize AI/ML models specifically and only to the extent necessary for those search functions.
* Display and Output: The presentation of the asset in the search output must include a direct reference or link to the original location. Verbatim excerpts or snippets may be displayed to assist users in evaluating the relevance of the result.

~~The Search category does not include uses that generate outputs which materially reduce the need to access the original asset.~~

comments.author: chrisn
comments.body:
Updated proposal, from Leah:

The use of one or more assets in a search application to direct users to the original location from which the assets were retrieved.

This category includes:

* The presentation of the asset in the search output must include a direct reference or link to the original location. To assist users in evaluating the relevance of the result, excerpts, or snippets may be displayed from the source asset.
* The internal processing of assets to perform indexing, ranking, and retrieval may include the use and training of AI/ML models, specifically for, and only to enable, the search application itself.


This category does not include:

* The asset(s) must not be used, ~~incorporated, summarized, aggregated, or reproduced~~ to generate summaries or other new content beyond excerpts or snippets, as referenced above.
* Evaluating an asset for potential use does not constitute use of the asset.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: @chrisn the evolution of that text is now [in the editors draft](https://ietf-wg-aipref.github.io/drafts/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab.html#name-search). Has that resolved this issue? Note that we can still discuss search, of course.

issues.title: "No preference" vs "unknown"
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

_From @chrisn in [email](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/2ZbEx73js_cTQT8mI1Wy6_0ZC_s):_

The "no preference" terminology could be misinterpreted as meaning that a website or content provider does not mind how their content is used (i.e., they don't have a preference either way). This would not be a valid assumption to make. It would be much more accurate to state that the preference is unknown. I recommend that the document aligns on the "allow", "disallow", and "unknown" statuses described in Section 5. This affects various parts of the draft:

* In Section 3, change "This can mean that no preference is stated for a given usage category" to "This can mean that the preference for a given usage category is unknown".

* In Section 3.2, which says "allow, disallow, or no preference"

* In Section 6, I suggest a rephrasing: "For example, the following states a preference to allow AI training (Section 4.2), disallow generative AI training (Section 4.3). The preference for categories other than subsets of these categories is unknown." (This would also fix the repeated "and" and "other" in the existing text.)

* In Section 6.5, "Otherwise, no preference is stated for that category of use" should be "Otherwise, the preference for that category of use is unknown".

* In Section 6.6, "A mapping might then define that no preference is associated with other categories" should be "A mapping might then define the preference associated with other categories is unknown."


### Proposed Resolution

_No response_

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: This seems pretty easy.  It's one of those tricks of English, where "no preference" and "no stated preference" mean something different.  The latter, or "unknown preference" as Chris suggests, is what we should be using.

comments.author: DNStories
comments.body:
I prefer "no preference indicated" or no stated preference to unknown. It signals that the content provider has provided no explicit instruction within the AIPref header.  
It's Farzaneh ... (I changed my name but it doesn't appear!)

comments.author: chrisn
comments.body: The reason I suggest unknown is that would make the rest of the document consistent with section 5, which describes the three potential answers of allow, disallow, and unknown.

issues.title: Follow-Up: Previously Raised Concern on Automated Processing category’s breadth, vagueness, and potential for harm
issues.author: kmadhavan-msft
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

This issue builds on concerns we raised earlier about the breadth and ambiguity of the automated processing category that we have previously [raised here](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues/169). Despite prior feedback, the latest draft still retains language that conflates unrelated behaviors and lacks enforceable semantics. To summarize our prior concern: 

The term “Automated Processing” in the current draft is too broad and ambiguous, risking unintended inclusion of ordinary, essential web operations. This overreach could jeopardize legitimate and safe internet functions by restricting non-AI crawlers and foundational automation that keeps the web usable. One critical point to consider here is that existing mechanisms provided under [RFC 9309](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html) already provide a well understood and viable mechanism to address the scenarios for which this category is intended in the first place. 

One additional observation to add is that we think that this term is not required and seems to have little support. The introduction of categories regarding training and outputs speaks to the crux of the concerns we hear from members of the working group and larger community. This begs the relevance of this “uber” category that may, as we indicate above, impact structural internet operations in ways that some do not anticipate.

### Proposed Resolution

Remove this high-level category completely. Given the edits already present in this draft, this category is largely unnecessary.

- #155

issues.title: Use of “fine-tune” in “Foundation AI Model Production” category
issues.author: kmadhavan-msft
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

The inclusion of “fine-tune” in the Foundation AI Model Production category (section 4.2 of draft version 4) is unnecessary and scientifically imprecise. Fine-tuning has a overly broad meaning dependent on context and is very hard to define. The term is ambiguous and context-dependent: in modern ML practice, fine-tuning can describe a wide range of techniques, from full parameter re-optimization to lightweight adapter or prompt-based adjustments, varying substantially by architecture and application. Treating it as a discrete category risks conflating routine adaptation with foundational training, creating ambiguity for implementers and misalignment with publisher intent.  

Importantly, this terminology was never raised or discussed in prior WG deliberations, and its late unnecessary introduction expands scope without clear consensus or definitional precision. This is also apparent in the fact that fine-tuning is never defined in the document. 

### Proposed Resolution

Remove the term fully and avoid confusion and ambiguity. Potentially rename the category as “Foundational AI Model Training and models refined from them” as “The act of using content to train large-scale, general-purpose generative AI models intended to enable broad capabilities, including the generation of text, images, and other synthetic content across diverse domains.”

Pedro Suarez: Fine-tuning can mean many things. If we worry just about production, it's easier to talk about. Are the weights changing? is the model itself changing? Is the model stable?

issues.title: Search should be a separate category, not nested under AI Output
issues.author: kmadhavan-msft
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

The current nesting of the “Search” category under “AI Output” introduces both conceptual and practical confusion. The argument we have repeatedly heard across the entire community seems to be that Search is a foundational web function that should remain clearly distinct from AI-generated outputs such as summaries, answers, or synthesized responses. The purpose of calling out “Search” explicitly seems to be aimed at preserving this distinction. If there must be a separate Search category based on rough consensus (still under debate) – it should not be nested under AI Output. 

More importantly, nesting Search under AI Output risks conflating these fundamentally different activities and could lead to user misunderstanding, where a publisher disables “AI Output” to restrict generative use but inadvertently also disables Search visibility. To maintain semantic clarity and prevent unintended consequences, “Search” should be elevated as its own category, separate from AI Output. 

### Proposed Resolution

Separate Search into its own category independent of AI output.

issues.title: Search category definition attempts to redefine established search behavior
issues.author: kmadhavan-msft
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

The current definition of the “Search” category attempts to require that “the asset can only be represented in the output with excerpts that are drawn verbatim from it”, but this conflicts with the well-established operational behavior of modern retrieval systems. Search results often feature generated or reworded snippets to give users relevant context, highlights, or support user intent.  Moreover, the definition appears to conflate “Search” with the “Exact Text Match” or “match-text” category defined in [A Vocabulary for Controlling Usage of Content Collected by Search and AI Crawlers](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-madhavan-aipref-displaybasedpref-01) rather than treating search as a distinct paradigm of retrieval. This conflation risks imposing display constraints on indexing and retrieval workflows that are not aligned with real-world practice. The vocabulary should reflect the intent to allow retrieval and access (for search) without prescribing how snippets or excerpts must be generated or displayed.

### Proposed Resolution

Remove the text regarding verbatim match completely and add the exact output match category as a sub-category to search. Additionally, we strongly recommend further work to iron out the definition for the search category itself given that existing options such as “noindex” exist and are widely adopted to completely opt out of search.

issues.title: Replace the Term “Client” with “User” to Avoid Ambiguity and Exposure of Internal System Details
issues.author: kmadhavan-msft
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

The draft repeatedly uses the term “client” in describing how content access and preference signaling occur. However, the term is ambiguous in this context. In standard web architecture, “client” can mean a wide range of entities – browsers, intermediaries, SDKs, or even subcomponents of larger systems. Within this specification, the word could inadvertently be interpreted as referring to the internal workings of AI systems or proprietary business secrets, rather than the end user. 

This ambiguity creates two key risks: 

1. **Interpretive confusion** – implementers may misread “client” as implying insight into internal system design rather than describing an external access actor. 
2. **Unintended disclosure ris**k – references to “clients” could be construed as exposing or requiring disclosure of proprietary AI or service internals that are outside the scope of the draft. 

In addition, the usage of the term “client” is inconsistent with the working group’s pivot toward output-based preferences, which focus on the representation and use of content in outputs rather than on the mechanisms or actors that perform access. Retaining “client” therefore risks re-anchoring the draft in the previous model that the group has intentionally evolved beyond. 

### Proposed Resolution

Replace “client” with a more neutral term such as “user”, which accurately captures the entity initiating access without implying any internal architecture.

comments.author: erinsimon
comments.body:
Agreed with this issue.  Extending the "output" category to clients of a system brings internal and intermediate processes back in scope of something that was intended to scope them out.  

I understand from in-person conversations that the concern is that intermediate steps in a multistep process might be operated by different organizations, and there is a desire not to allow preferences to get lost along the chain of operations on its way to an end-user.  I think there's a simpler way to do that, like for example to have a single sentence that these preferences apply at the user-facing step, and prior steps must ensure that the preference is communicated through the entire chain.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: See also #167.

comments.author: chrisn
comments.body: In terms of grounding or RAG type usage, preferences need to apply at the step that does the actual processing and not any downstream system.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
This might be overtaken by events.  "client" doesn't appear in the current draft at all.

I think that this was probably raised in the context of the "AI output" term, where @kmadhavan-msft used the word "user" and after discussion I changed it to "client".  It wasn't clear that was the right thing to do and that opened up some very difficult questions about what the meaning of "AI output" was (along with a number of similarly difficult questions, I recall).  I think we're in the clear for now.

issues.title: Search Cateogry May Lead to Unintended Effects
issues.author: joncaldon
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

We are still left with a Search category that may not reflect how modern Search engines operate today, let alone how they may operate in the near future. While I understand that the purpose of this group is to define a vocabulary, and not to embody policy, it is nonetheless better to define a vocabulary that people can understand and that reflects reality, so that those preferences, once expressed, can be respected in meaningful ways.

Specifically, there are references to “traditional” Search which might lead publishers to think that current Search implementations are merely, say, 1998-era Search with additional AI parts bolted to that infrastructure in a way that can be separated. But that is incorrect. 

To take one example, if Search results are to be grouped under headings to give users an idea of the various kinds of results that exist for a particular query, and those headings are generated by AI, with reference to the links grouped thereunder, that would seem to fall outside the Search category as written, even if the links-and-snippets part of the results is otherwise satisfactory. A publisher expressing a “traditional-Search-only” preference would find themselves outside these grouped links, perhaps, and perhaps not appearing with the prominence they would desire.

Suggest we make clear that Search=yes also encompasses this kind of thing, or, alternatively, that we explain to publishers that if Search=yes remains narrowly defined, that unexpected outcomes are a real risk both now and as products evolve in the future. 


### Proposed Resolution

_No response_
