issues.title: Remove the vocabulary document and enable a market for content rights documents
issues.author: jwrosewell
issues.body:
## Current State

There are two documents this group are considering which I summarize as:

- ATTACH – a method of communicating content usage signals.
- VOCAB – definitions concerning content usage restrictions.

ATTACH seems to be nearly complete and sensible as it relates wholly to engineering and the signaling associated with content usage restrictions.  

VOCAB does not relate to engineering but standardizing usage agreements between content owners and receivers. The goal of such standardization is to help reduce friction when communicating with disparate websites about specific use rights.

## Problems

1.	The approach of VOCAB lacks fidelity and flexibility.

Whilst it might be convenient for engineers to reduce copyright and licensing to a few short sentences the reality is much more complex. The current approach will restrict the options available for other professions who wish to use language that might have specific legal or contractual meaning. Any restricted list will be anticompetitive.

2.	The current VOCAB proposal focuses on technology and not use cases. 

As just one current example it discusses whether to contribute or not to foundational model building whilst neglecting the uses that the resulting model will be put to. The same model used with AI overviews is a very different uses then accessibility solutions.

3. 	robots.txt is only one of many mediums via which licenses for content might be communicated.

Another challenge is that the VOCAB is geared towards robot scripts by inclusion solely within robots.txt, rather than applying to AI foundational model building, training, enhancements even if the Generative AI is embedded into either a consumer-facing browser or a publisher partner.

## Proposal

I propose the group agrees to replace the VOCAB document with immutable URL documents containing content usage text to address the problems that are well documented and referenced in the end note.

Recipients of these URLs will maintain a table of uses that they deem are allowable based on a human reading the associated content usage document. The following table is an example.

| Content Usage Document URL | Usage |
| - | - |
| https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-02#name-automated-processing-catego | Automated Processing |
| https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-02#name-ai-training-category | AI Training |
| https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-02#name-generative-ai-training-cate	| Generative AI Training |
| https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-02#name-ai-use-category | AI Use |
| https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-02#name-search-category | Search |

When a new URL is received it will be added to this table by the receiver for review and classification. The receiver might wish to determine the order that URLs are reviewed based on frequency of use by content rights holders.

This aspect of the proposal is out of scope for the group and is provided purely for illustration only as it is for each individual receiver of content to decide how they respond to the content usage document pointed to by the URL.

A content owner that sought to introduce their own content usage text/document would be free to create their own. For example; I might produce a content usage document that required payment for use of my content with AI using the URL `https://rosewell.me/ai-payment-for-content`.

Example

If my prior example URL where used with ATTACH example showing a robots.txt at 3.4 could be modified to become.

```
	User-Agent: *
	Allow: /
	Disallow: /never/
	Content-Usage: /ai-ok-with-payment/ https://rosewell.me/ai-payment-for-content
	User-Agent: ExampleBot
	Allow: /
	Content	-Usage: https://rosewell.me/ai-payment-for-content 
```

## Modifications

The ATTACH document would need to be simplified to remove the `=n` and `=y` notation. This would no longer be needed because the presence of the URL indicates that the associated document applies to content usage. Determining what is allowed or not allowed for each document will be a matter for the parties involved. The absence of the URL would mean nothing can be assumed.

A further modification to ATTACH is to require the URL provided to never change once published.

## Benefits

There is ample precedence for this proposal within the field of engineering. Open-source software flourished because it offered standardized terms to all recipients, reducing costs and complexity via its vocabulary of popular contract templates (i.e. MPL, MIT, Apache, etc). We should be careful limiting extensibility by attempting to adopt a centralized vocabulary, without allowing copyright holders to choose how to govern their property (e.g., much like selecting which of many open-source contracts a rights holder offers its property to recipients). With this extensibility many open-source license agreements flourished, and then the industry settled on a relatively small number. It is worth noting that any open-source author is still free to use their own license if they don’t wish to use a common one.

With such a modification to VOCAB terms and locations a group of lawyers from publishers and AI companies in a given region might come together to define a common content usage document using methods and skills not available to the IETF. This document might become a commonly referenced standard contract.

Publishers and AI companies in other regions might modify content usage documents to support laws or requirements in their regions.

Medium’s that don’t use robots.txt would be able to use the same content-usage documents. For example; a `<div>` tag in HTML might have a specific content usage document that can be assigned to it indicating different requirements to other elements on the web page.

With this approach the IETF will cease to be involved in defining restrictive language but offer a consistent framework for automated negotiation. Various parties associated with content ownership and usage will be free to define, iterate, and use many agreements using whatever language or process they wish within a standardized framework.

The direction supports the development of standard contractual clauses by any entity.

## Compatible

For those that wish to retain usage of the VOCAB definitions that the group has created to date they would simply modify the table at section 6.1 to use a URL that references their text. Using the existing URL as an example the following tables shows the modification.

| Category | Content Usage Document URL |
| - | - |
| Automated Processing | https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-02#name-automated-processing-catego |
| AI Training | https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-02#name-ai-training-category |
| Generative AI Training | https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-02#name-generative-ai-training-cate |
| AI Use | https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-02#name-ai-use-category |
| Search |	https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-02#name-search-category |

With such a change it would be for the market to decide if these definitions were useful or not without being constrained by IETF processes and practices.

## Questions & Challenges

### - Doesn’t the current draft already supports this capability?

The draft changes frequently so this can’t be answer until a final version is ready. However even if this were possible we need to be mindful that when a technical mechanism becomes widely adopted by dominant companies the possibility of utilizing additional choices and features becomes impractical.

### - Doesn’t this mean rightsholders won’t have a mechanism to communicate preferences for AI training and/or use?

No. The document referred to by the URL will determine what rights the rightsholder grants to the recipient. The recipient will need to inspect that document and determine what they are permitted to do, or not do. 

Market forces will likely settle on a practical narrow set of common documents after a period of experimentation, trial and error, and innovation.

### - This proposal will make it impossible to share a common set of terminology and definitions.

No. It will be for market forces to determine which documents get used and which don’t rather than the IETF. If the market wants a set of common definitions and terminology then they will create those documents and they will become adopted.

It can be reasonably expected that a broad number of documents will be created initially with a smaller number becoming adopted and refined for different use cases over time. This happened in open source licensing.

### - How does this proposal create bounded choices that engineers can work with?

Bounding restricts choices. Whilst that might be desirable in technical protocols it is not how business works. Businesses must be free to make their own choices. Unaltered the direction of this group will restrict business choice in practice via bounded lists defined by engineers. That must be avoided if the work is to be successful.

In this proposal some bounding is achieved via market forces and disciplines other than engineering and an IETF VOCAB document. 

Bounding is achieved over time in practice rather than at the outset via defined vocabularies.

### - IETF documents can be changed over time. Why doesn’t this proposal recognize this?

Market participants must be free to decide the terms under which they make their property available to others and not be constrained, including by IETF processes for document control.

### - Human review of documents and URLs will be required.

Possibly, although AIs might be able to help. 

In any case there is human review now. This proposal simply moves the human review from an IETF group like this one where consensus is achieved among a group of predominantly engineering people, to many disciplines and people.

### - The volume of possible documents will be impractical.

The incentives for the market are to keep the number of content usage documents used in practice to an optimum number. That will be for the market to decide and will likely follow a pattern of rapid expansion and then contraction. 

If a new content usage document is “minted” and used by only one publisher that is of little interest to AI companies then it will not be classified and the content will be ignored by the AI company. 

However, if that one publisher is successful in persuading many publishers to use the same content usage document then it might become more popular over time and AI companies might then decide to invest the effort in classifying it so that they can consider how they might use the associated content. That is a significant benefit of the proposal.

### - Content owners could mount a Denial of Service (DOS) attach on AIs via many new documents.

The DOS example is mitigated via incentives. If the publishers have an incentive to create so many documents as to overwhelm AIs then it would be a sign that the market is not functioning for publishers and AI companies will need to change their practices. This is a matter for markets and not the IETF.

### - Content rights documents could be poorly written and inconsistent.

It is entirely possible content usage documents will be poorly written and inconsistent. In such situation's they are unlikely to be used. See the [NASA Open Source Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Open_Source_Agreement) in the field of open-source licensing as an example of such a document.

It is also possible some will be well written and become widely used. See the [MIT open-source licence](https://opensource.org/license/MIT).

### - Content rights documents may not be clear meaning the outcome for those reviewing the document could be “unknown”.

Well drafted documents form common contractual clauses in many fields. Consider for example standard contractual clauses for data transfers between EU and non-EU countries.

Suitably qualified and motivated people would produce content usage documents that are clear. Of course, if only unqualified people with little motivation work on the problem, then "unknown" would be a likely outcome. If that happens then it would show businesses are not really interested in solving the problem. I consider that unlikely given my understanding of the issues.

Neither outcome is a failure for this group.
 
### - Are you proposing that standards take on a limited role and simple enable arbitrary statements to be carried?

Yes. The problem the vocabulary seeks to address is not one for the IETF. It is a business problem for business people.

### - Technical standards taking a limited role is a gamble where we’re betting that there is an interest in creating a market for common rights documents.

That is no different to the gamble we are all taking spending time writing and reading these emails and issues. If there is no market for the work of this group, then it will have failed. If there is a limited group of market participants who will benefit from the acknowledged restricted options, and a long process to remedy these restrictions for others via IETF processes, then the group will have failed in practice. In all fields some participants win when choice for others is restricted. It is for that reason we must not restrict business choice via a vocabulary.

Given the level of interest in this group and the importance of the problem to so many constituent groups enabling them to experiment by creating a market for them to do so will result in the best outcomes for the market over time.

In short; the IETF can setup the conditions for others to innovate; and then get out of the way.

## Related Issues

Adopting this proposal would address the following issues by making them out of scope for IETF and the subject of flexible usage documents created and stewarded by many organizations and not the IETF.

issues.title: Consider content owner brand use and endorsement
issues.author: jwrosewell
issues.body:
AI firms (such as Answer Engines) desire a standardized signaling mechanism for online copyright owners to communicate the specific rights they are granting regarding the use of their copyrighted material. Because copyright law mandates explicit permission rather than an opt-out process, publishers should not need to take any restrictive measures to prevent undesired competing uses.  

A minimal but effective framework should allow media owners to specify three distinct categories of use:

1.	Source link inclusion in search results (SERP): The media owner may authorize the display of titles, snippets, and URLs for audiences to discover their online properties, and condition such use on specific remuneration methods and amounts. The generally accepted default for online listings to aid discovery and navigation is free use of the navigation link (URL) and publication of the media owner’s summary via the <title></title> and <meta name="description"> tags. 
•	Today this is signaled via <meta name="robots" content="index"> or content=”noindex” 
•	Additional signals include:  Noindex, Index, Follow, Nofollow, Noimageindex, None, Noarchive, Nocache, Nosnippet, Unavailable_after.
•	Given “index” was designed solely for SERP, this vocabulary needs to distinguish DISPLAY vs NODISPLAY in SERP, rather than the technical method a search engine or directly listing service might use to include the link and media owner’s summary of their property.

2.	Generative use: The media owner may authorize the use of their content for model training, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), or other methods that produce competitive generative outputs, and condition such use on specific remuneration methods and amounts. Instead of focusing on the technical methods (e.g., cache, index) that will change over time, media owners should focus on purposes of output use regardless of technical method.
•	Such allow/permit or disallow/prohibit signals must control 
o	WHO: access management
o	WHAT: asset designation
o	HOW MUCH: payment methods and pricing per purpose/use (see https://rslstandard.org/rsl)
o	FOR WHAT: purposes (e.g., generation, classification, summarisation, embedding, attribution, onward sharing with others for any of these licensed uses)
o	HOW LONG: expiration date
o	DECLARATIONS: legal disclaimers about what is licensed 

3.	Brand endorsement/attribution: The media owner may authorize use of its trademarks or brand identity alongside generative content outputs, including separate forms of RAG that connect outputs with identifiable publisher branding, and condition such use on specific remuneration methods and amounts.
•	Although endorsement for AI system output is a subset of the purpose/use in 2. above, this is important an important aspect as one can image brand endorsement may altering payment and usage if included in AI system outputs. As such each purpose/use is not stand alone, but also requires logic for combinations (e.g., endorsement link without use in generation or endorsement link with use in generation). 

Ensuring flexibility for augmenting the standard distinct signals will enable AI and search systems to honor license boundaries faithfully while maintaining transparency, competition, and respect for copyright. RSL already includes such extensibility in its protocol and should be adopted into the IETF proposal.

issues.title: Introduction: relation to existing laws
issues.author: mgendler
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

It is clear from the debate in this working group over the past year that there is significant confusion about what legal implications, if any, the work of this group is aiming to have on creators globally. 

For example, the text of the current vocab draft ([draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-05](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-05.html)) says that it “is intended to be used in jurisdictions where expressing preferences results in legal obligations … without prejudice to applicable laws …,” but it is completely unclear (and silent about) what jurisdictions, legal obligations, or laws that it is referring to, exactly. 

Obviously, this working group, as part of a technical standards body, is not trying to hijack the role of a legislature or regulator.  It is not appropriate for us to design standards that may affect legal protections that millions of creators across the world have with relation to their countries’ domestic copyright, contract, and other laws. 

To make it clear that this working group is not aiming to override copyright owners’ existing legal protections in their respective countries, or to override creators’ existing terms of service, I propose to clarify the language in the introductory section.

I think that clarity will also improve uptake of the standardized language, better fulfilling the objectives of this WG. 

This issue applies to the vocabulary document (including some sections later on other than the introduction) and we should pursue similar clarification for the attachment document, to be clear that nothing in that document has any legal effect either - but I'll leave that for future issue submissions. 

### Proposed Resolution

I propose starting by strengthening language in the introductory section.
 
It currently reads:

>    including the applicability of exceptions and limitations to
>    Copyright.

> For clarity, expressing preferences is without prejudice to applicable laws,

>  in a website’s Terms of Use (or comparable page), and in the event of any conflict

issues.title: Carrying preferences with stuff
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

@TimidRobot points out that we don't really talk about our expectations around how preferences might be carried along with the stuff (currently, "assets") that they apply to.

I think that our presumption thus far was that anyone who acquires covered stuff carries metadata for that stuff along with it so that any use can be informed by preferences.  This means carrying robots.txt or headers, for the attachments we are using.

### Proposed Resolution

This might be tricky, but I think that our expectation is that metainformation and preferences live with the things that they cover.  That is going to be hard for things like robots.txt, which might not naturally follow along with the bytes.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Something that was noted about this is that any acquisition that is for a specific purpose can discard stuff that has preference that are incompatible with that use.

issues.title: Proposed revision of search category to focus on "substantial" generative use
issues.author: erinsimon
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

There has been substantial debate about how to define a search category that can be used to express a preference for use in traditional forms of search results without including the newer more [narrative overviews ](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues/102)that have been introduced in the last few years.  

Articulating this distinction is [tricky](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues/98) for a few reasons: 
- Traditional search results are the [result of AI processes](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues/173), so the category cannot disclaim all AI use or the input of content to AI systems.
- Traditional search results may involve some amount of [non-verbatim copying](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues/181), such as eliding or mildly rewording text to better highlight relevant aspects.
- The category is not intended to prohibit categorization and labeling of traditional search results, but an overly strict prohibition on generated content could cover the generation of very short category labels.
- Referring instead to "summaries" does not provide sufficient clarity about how much or what kind of generated output is permissible.  Referring instead to the [potential to substitute for the asset](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues/150) begs legal questions as well as introduces ambiguity in scope.
- Requiring the asset to be linked to in the output presumes that the asset will be relevant to the output, and could be interpreted to mean that the output cannot be evaluated for inclusion without a guarantee that the asset is included. 

What is needed is a definition that focuses on the core distinction of the use of the asset as an input to the generation of more than very short amounts of content, but allows for some flexibility in quoting, categorizing, and labeling.  This proposal describes that as "substantial" amounts of "new" content, and as an initial proposal defines substantial to mean sentence-level text.  A numerical threshold could be used instead, but it would have to account for the differences in semantic density between languages.

It is also necessary to harmonize this category with the beneficial uses mentioned in the preamble and the working group discussions, to ensure that it does not impede the accessibility of content through AI-mediated means.  Thus the category clarifies that transforming the modality of the content (e.g., text to speech, translation) is not in scope of the category preference.

This is, of course, a starting point for further discussion.  Please suggest improvements!

### Proposed Resolution

Replace the Search category with the following: 

**Non-Generative Search:** Using the asset in search results, where the asset is not used as an input to the generation of a substantial amount of new content.
- Substantial means sentence-level text, images of any size, and audiovisual content of any length.
- Search results are the links and associated content presented to users of a search application.
- Transcription, translation, and speech-to-text do not constitute new content.
- Evaluating an asset for potential use does not constitute use of the asset.
- This category also permits use of the asset to produce the models that are used in the search application.

comments.author: paul2keller
comments.body:
Hi @erinsimon thanks for sharing this. This seems like a genuinely useful approach to defining the search category (by distinguishing from generative search outputs). However I feel that this (and especially the last bullet point) risks removing the ability to express the classic `train-ai=n` `search=y` combination that we have been circling around here a lot. 

To me it seems that the "also permits use of the asset to produce the models that are used in the search application" would in effect mean that you can use the asset to train any model that is used as part of the search application. This would in effect mean if a search operator somehow uses a foundation models (say Gemini in your case) as part of the search process `non-Generative Search=y` would in effect also mean `train-ai=y` for that particular model. Is that indeed what you intend here?

I am aware that the current draft contains a similar provision in the definition of `search` ("includes any training that is necessary to produce models used in the search application") which feels a bit more targeted (the "necessary" is doing some real constraining work here), although it presents pretty much the same issue: if the use of a model is necessary then it would overrule the a `train-ai=n` preference for that model.  

It seems to me that any such clause would ideally be restricted to models whose function is limited to retrieval or ranking within the pipeline, not generative models deployed in search.

comments.author: erinsimon
comments.body:
Hi Paul,

My intention was just to track the provision in the draft definition of search that you mention.  It was just oversight not to use the word "necessary," and I'd be fine including that in this definition.

I think there's a good discussion to be had about limitations on what training is included in a search category (mine or the operative draft's).  Ranking and retrieval aren't enough to operate non-generative search features, though.  As one example, the search engine must also be taught to understand queries and content before the latter can be ranked for the former.  And it would be important to define generative with regard to usage rather than capabilities, because generative capabilities can be a byproduct of training models to be able to understand inputs.

Other than that, does the definition work for you?  Can we add it to the agenda for next week?

comments.author: paul2keller
comments.body: thanks for the clarification @erinsimon. The agenda is maintained by @mnot and @sureshkrishnan so that is up to them, but I think it makes sense to discuss this.

comments.author: tymrtn
comments.body:
The difficulty articulating this definition is a symptom of a missing use class.

AI Overviews and similar products are not search — they are public inference with a search UI. Forcing that use into a patched search category requires substantiality thresholds ("sentence-level text") that are language-dependent, output-focused rather than act-focused, and already contested.

If inference-time generative use had its own use class, `search` could be defined cleanly: retrieval and presentation of an asset with attribution, without generating new content from it. No threshold needed.

Also flagging: the final bullet ("this category also permits use of the asset to produce the models used in the search application") embeds a training permission inside the search category without calling it that. That scope expansion should be explicit and separate.

comments.author: tymrtn
comments.body:
When you search Google today, two different things can happen:

1. Google shows you a list of links to websites, with short excerpts from each page.
2. Google writes you a paragraph answering your question, drawn from those websites.

These proposals treats both as "search." They are not the same. In case 1, 
the website gets traffic. In case 2, the user never visits the website. 
That is the harm publishers are trying to prevent — and it needs its own 
category, not a footnote in the search definition.

Also: the last bullet gives permission to train AI models on your content 
as part of allowing "search." That should be a separate, explicit permission.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
A few things:

> Evaluating an asset for potential use does not constitute use of the asset.

Could this be "Allowing search includes evaluating assets for potential use, even if those assets are not selected."  That is, rather than excluding ranking from the category, explicitly include it.

> This category also permits use of the asset to produce the models that are used in the search application.

I think that I heard Erin concede this already, but this might be better as "Including the asset in the training of models that are exclusively used by the non-generative search application."

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: @erinsimon I _think_ this has been overcome by events -- OK to close?

issues.title: Secondary Purpose
issues.author: gitnnelg
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

The WG has discussed following a purpose based foundation of expressing preferences.     A consequence of formulating preferences based on purpose is what is the WG's expectation on secondary purpose uses.  

If the WG does choose to follow a purpose based preferences vocabulary, then it should clearly document its expected approach to secondary uses.      

There would be a couple of different approaches that could be chosen by the WG (this is not a complete list)

1.  An option is that no secondary use is expected or allowed, without the need to express it explicitly
2. Another option, would be to add an explicit declaration on secondary uses.



### Proposed Resolution

_No response_

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I'm not following what you are intending here:

* If there is a preference defined in our vocabulary (or a vocabulary that all the entities involve understand), then that preference can be conveyed.
* No preference is stated if no preference is stated, either because there is no preference or because the stated preference uses a vocabulary term that is not understood by the recipient.

That is, there is no such thing as "secondary use" in this system.  To imply that there might be is not consistent with what we are defining.

As noted in #167, preferences apply to all uses, not the acquisition of stuff.  I don't see how this issue would be actionable.

comments.author: gitnnelg
comments.body:
If the focus shifts to declaring preferences for specific uses as in done in other frameworks, then a common question that arises is _what about secondary use that is desired or comes about for the data after the initial use?_         

In PII handling situations the mainstream rule is that secondary uses that were not included in the original data purpose declared to the PII owner at the time of permission granting by the PII owner are not allowed and would require a new permission.

While AI-Pref is not a strict permission grant, but is an expression of preference the question arises of what is the expected behavior from the users accessing the data, when their purpose for the data grows beyond the original access.    

There are several use-cases to then cover:

1. If the full AI-Pref expression from the original access has been retained and has the new purpose listed, then that is straighforward, since the preferences for the new purpose are available in the retained AI-Pref expression.
2. If the AI-Pref expression was discarded after the original access, then the user should be directed to re-obtain the AI-Pref via a new request.

the core issue here involves not preferences applying to all uses, but the situation where the past preferences have not been retrained, while the use of the data is being put to a new purpose.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
A user that has a new use in mind would consult the preferences associated with the assets they have.  If the preferences apply to that use, then they have information about preferences.  If not, then they learn nothing.

Obviously, if they discard information at the point of collection because they believe it to be irrelevant at the time (they were only collecting data for a search engine, not arbitrary model training to give one example) then that would be their fault and they probably can't assume that no preferences were expressed later when they check.  Otherwise, this is not very difficult: there is a preference only if there is a preference.

comments.author: gitnnelg
comments.body: based upon other changes to the architecture since submitted, I believe this can now be closed.

issues.title: Foundation Models are too specific
issues.author: mnot
issues.body: In Toronto, Paul expresses concern that FM excludes use cases that people want to express preferences about, and suggests broadening so that there isn't a distinction.

comments.author: tymrtn
comments.body:
"Foundation model" captures the high-profile cases but leaves a gap that bad actors can drive through. A company can train a task-specific model on unlicensed content and argue it falls outside the preference because it's not a foundation model. "AI model" closes that gap.

An AI model is a computational artifact whose outputs are determined by parameters derived from training data, rather than by explicit programming. This includes language models, image generation models, audio models, video models, code models, and multimodal models.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
The following text was the outcome of a discussion from a small team:

The production or refinement of the weights of a general purpose model that can generate content in one or more modalities (text, image, audio, etc...) or a specialized model that is designed to generate content in one or more modalities.

<details>
<summary>
Notes:
</summary>

* This splits the definition in two deliberately.  The general purpose model side is based on its capabilities; the specialized model is based on its purpose.  This addresses concerns about this definition sweeping in specialized models (like those used in email filters, say) because they might have (unused) capabilities.
* In saying "generate content", the intent is to exclude classifiers or models that produce simple metrics (yes/no answers, probabilities, or labels).

</details>

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
A more streamlined version of the same text, that removes the split might be:

The production or refinement of the weights of a model that can generate content in one or more modalities (text, image, audio, etc...).

comments.author: sureshkrishnan
comments.body:
In the poll during the Toronto interim, we polled for

Text A: The production or refinement of the weights of a general purpose model that can generate content in one or more modalities (text, image, audio, etc...) or a specialized model that is designed to generate content in one or more modalities.

Text B: The production or refinement of the weights of a model that can generate content in one or more modalities (text, image, audio, etc...).

and there was no clear preference for either.

comments.author: llemeurfr
comments.body:
In principle, these definitions should be understandable to content providers (a.k.a. copyright holders) willing to express their preferences. Technical jargon like "weights" is problematic in this regard. Companion documents may contain more technical details, produced by the group, or not.  

From yesterday's discussion, it appears that it is technically impossible to precisely define what a foundation model is or what a generative model is (I heard that every AI model can "generate content", and what is substitutive is heavily subjective). Putting a preference on the use of content for training "AI models" at large appears to be the only level on which both parties can agree. 

A specificity of an IA model is that it is not 100% programmed (not totally rules-based) and therefore relies on training on large datasets. Which is exactly what content providers may want to opt out of. Can we create a definition based on this characteristic?

comments.author: sureshkrishnan
comments.body: After further discussion at the Toronto interim there was a clear preference to use the text "The production or refinement of the weights of a general purpose model that can generate content in one or more modalities (text, image, audio, etc...) or a specialized model that is designed to generate content in one or more modalities." as the starting point.

comments.author: kelleyk-ant

issues.title: Add use-case matrix artifact for train-ai/search overlap classification
issues.author: altanai
issues.body:
I think the current AIPREF category definitions for `train-ai` and `search` need tighter boundary behavior in edge cases, especially where workflows involve retrieval, summarization, and mixed pipelines. This creates ambiguity for implementers and reviewers when categories overlap.

Related discussions already exist, but they do not provide a shared test matrix artifact for classification consistency:
- https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues/196
- https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues/172
- https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues/150

I propose to create a dedicated use-case matrix artifact (appendix or companion markdown) that tests expected behavior per category and overlap precedence.

## Initial Edge-Case Scenarios
- Search retrieval with snippets only (no model update)
- Search retrieval feeding grounding for generated answer
- Search result ranking model continuously updated from click logs
- User-supplied content in prompt plus crawler-sourced context
- Crawler-sourced corpus used for test-time adaptation
- RAG pipeline with caching of embeddings derived from content
- Search display where AI transforms excerpts for accessibility

issues.title: Use-Case Matrix Artifact for Train-AI/Search
issues.author: altanai
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

I think the current AIPREF category definitions for `train-ai` and `search` need tighter boundary behavior in edge cases, especially where workflows involve retrieval, summarization, and mixed pipelines. This creates ambiguity for implementers and reviewers when categories overlap.

Related discussions already exist, but they do not provide a shared test matrix artifact for classification consistency:
- https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues/196
- https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues/172
- https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues/150

### Proposed Resolution

I propose to create a dedicated use-case matrix artifact (appendix or companion markdown) that tests expected behavior per category and overlap precedence.

## Edge-Case Scenarios
- Search retrieval with snippets only (no model update)
- Search retrieval feeding grounding for generated answer
- Search result ranking model continuously updated from click logs
- User-supplied content in prompt plus crawler-sourced context
- Crawler-sourced corpus used for test-time adaptation
- RAG pipeline with caching of embeddings derived from content
- Search display where AI transforms excerpts for accessibility

PS : This does not introduce new categories, only validates current category behavior

## Suggested matrix columns:

* Scenario ID
* Input source (crawler discovered / user provided / hybrid)
* Processing stage (indexing / ranking / retrieval / grounding / generation / model update)
* Output behavior (link-only / snippet / summary / generated answer)
* Categories triggered (search, train-ai, other)
* Declared preferences
* Expected effective result
* Rationale (with spec section reference)
* Ambiguity note (if any)

issues.title: Use of "synthetic" in AI definitions
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
### Confirmation

- [x] I have reviewed our [existing issues](https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/issues?q=state%3Aopen) and this issue is not present there.
- [x] I have read and understand the [IETF NOTE WELL](https://www.ietf.org/about/note-well/).

### Issue Description

Both @lrosenthol and @chrisn identified the word "synthetic" as being somewhat objectionable in the following definition of AI Training (from #211):

> Using an asset to modify the learned parameters of an AI model that is used to generate **synthetic** content in one or more modalities.

(Emphasis mine.)

This phrasing, "an AI model that is used to generate (synthetic) content in one or more modalities" is likely to be part of other vocabulary definitions we build.  So, while my sense is that the objection is not very strong, it is worth getting this right.

---

For reference, a dictionary defines "synthetic" (adj.) as:

1. Relating to, involving, or of the nature of synthesis.
2. Produced by synthesis, especially not of natural origin.
3. Prepared or made artificially.

### Proposed Resolution

No concrete recommendation from me; I just want a resolution.

Arguments in favor of removal presented thus far are centered on the view that the word is redundant or immaterial. @chrisn suggests that using the word leaves another place where meaning and interpretation are open to debate.

From my reading of the definitions above, an AI model inarguably produces synthetic content, likely following definition 3. The origin of any AI output is always artificial, unless it is reduced to a copy of material from a single natural source.  That's not a useful thing.  Once multiple sources are copied, that is synthesis.

So I don't think that the meaning can be ambiguous in any way.  However, the question of redundancy remains.

Even if it is redundant, the arguments in favor of retaining "synthetic" seem to reduce to a belief that it is an important emphasis.

issues.author: ekr-ietf

### Issue Description

_No response_

### Proposed Resolution

_No response_

comments.author: ekr-ietf
comments.body:
Post PR#220, the draft says:

> Servers MUST retain any preferences associated with a request if the content of that request is used to answer later requests. For example, the content of a PUT request that is used to answer subsequent GET requests. Note that servers that have not been updated to understand this field will not comply with this requirement.


In retrospect, I'm not sure what "retain" means, but arguably it means "propagate", so if I upload some asset with a given preference that must be provided whenever the asset is served. 

This actually seems problematic in several specific respects:

1. What if the asset is not served directly but rather mixed with other assets? This could happen if it's subsequently used for inference but also if it's just fed into some other process. For example, suppose that someone uploads a meme template with a permissive set of preferences and then I ask the system to do a face swap with a face with a less permissive set of preferences. What preferences should be served?

2. It seems like there is no way to provide different permissions to the site where you are uploading content than are provided when the content is served. For example, I might upload a photo to a social media site and be willing to let *them* train on it (potentially because it's part of the TOS) but then not want them to pass on that preference.



It also seems anomalous that clients are permitted to ignore these preferences but servers are required to propagate them.

More broadly, I'm not quite sure how this is supposed to work. The two dominant ways in which users upload content are (1) via a Web browser and (2) via apps. In the app case, it seems unlikely the user will be allowed to set HTTP headers directly, and the app can figure out its own way to propagate the user's preferences (assuming it wants to). I suppose it's possible that on the Web we would specify some kind of DNT/GPC-like header that the user could set in a browser preference, but that seems like it's more likely than not to lead to really widespread ignoring of the header.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Correct #220 changes that text to:

> Servers can use any preferences associated with a request if the content of that request is used to answer later requests. For example, attached preferences for a PUT request, where the content that is used to answer subsequent GET requests, might be copied to the response to those GET requests.

Does that change your position?  Because you seem to be concerned about the same things as in #168, which #220 addressed. The old text you quote was clearly bad when considering the vocabulary discussions we've had; it was mostly just outdated.

Basically, the new text is really just a reminder to maybe consider preferences attached to requests, especially when the content of those requests is later served.

comments.author: ekr-ietf
comments.body: Sorry, I somehow thought that #220 had merged. I agree the new text is superior and now largely harmless. With that said, I think my last point remains. As a practical matter, how do you expect clients to send the preference indication.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The content-usage header field can be included in requests and responses both.  In re-reading the text, it might be worth saying how *clients* can also use the value received in a response.  It's weird to talk about servers only, when the expectation is that clients are the ones who are expected to use the information.

comments.author: ekr-ietf
comments.body:
I was focusing on the server because in the example you provided something that is in a PUT is remembered in a subsequent GET, which seems to be a case of the server remembering.

As far as the client using the value, it seems like there are broadly two cases:

1. Automated AI-based clients.
2. Other ordinary clients (e.g., normal browsers)

The former are the subject of this document so I think that's clear and this text doesn't bear on that. I don't understand how the latter would work at all. Do you somehow have in mind that when a browser downloads an asset it should store the preferences and then replay them on future PUT/POSTs?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
As a browser-maker, I can't imagine doing anything with preferences in a browser.  That said, that's based on what I think is a consideration of the preferences in relation to what a browser is for (that is, a browser is a *user* agent).  Anything that we pass on to our users can't really capture preferences in a way that will survive most user flows, including viewing web pages, content on those pages, and file downloads.  As you well know, we can expose information in debugging interfaces, but most users have no use for those capabilities.

On the other hand, that's not a judgment that necessarily holds for web applications that fetch stuff that have this header field.  The Fetch API will expose the header field value, so those web applications can make their own judgment.  The same is true for other client software, like a curl integration in an app.

I tend to think that this is fine.  I don't think that anyone really expects a browser to do anything special here.  That it is possible to seek out and pay attention to preferences seems to be sufficient.  I'd be curious if anyone thinks that this is an unreasonable position.

issues.title: Does direct provision include URLs?
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
In discussions about AI use, the definition we considered was something like this:

> Use of an asset as input to a generative AI model,
> where the asset is not directly provided by the user.

## In favor of references

This wording leaves it ambiguous about whether a URL is direct.  Two options were floated, neither of which got a sufficiently positive response.

The first suggestion was to clarify that a URL can be used explicitly by adding something like ", either as a URL or by supplying the asset itself".

The second was a less explicit, focusing instead on what is necessary to go from a prompt that includes a reference to the asset.  In this version, the line would be drawn by saying that where inference is needed to determine what to feed into the model, that cannot be direct.

In this second model, it's possible that some statements could be recognized as unambiguous references that would not need interpretation.  For example "the Google homepage" as a string is not ambiguous.  Nor would the typo of "the Googgle homepage" be ambiguous, and it would meet this "user-supplied" test f a simple process that did not involve AI could recognize that.

Example text for that version was: "If a system needs to perform inference in order to determine which asset to use, that does not qualify as a user directly providing the asset."

A concern with that language was that it was potentially circular, in that the "inference" part would have to defined and that might lead to referencing the "AI Use" term.

In either case, the general arguments in favor of this focused on user convenience.  Providing a URL potentially saves a user (or their agent/browser) from having to acquire the asset and feed it to the model.

## In favor of forbidding references
 
The alternative is to say that "direct" means that this only covers the case where the bytes of the asset is supplied as input.

Potential text for this could be "Directly providing an asset does not include identifying the asset, such as by naming it or by providing a URL.  Users need to supply the literal asset as input directly."

The strongest argument here was an attention economy-based one.  Publishers were concerned that supplying a URL would mean that no human would ever see the content, denying them a potential opportunity to engage with a user.

---

It was also observed that the attachment mechanisms we are defining would naturally be stripped when supplying an asset directly in this way.  Only embedded metadata (and maybe registries) would be able to inform the AI system of the preference in this case.  Whatever the decision we make here, that's a factor we might consider acknowledging.

pulls.title: Define an exemplary format
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
As discussed, we want to define a recommended format.  This executes on that.  It uses Structured Fields, which will ensure that we have a very easy translation to HTTP fields.  It also fits neatly into the other formats we are considering.

There are some interesting implications that are worth highlighting. The text I've added goes into some of that in more detail, but just to list them for visibility:

* This is a sequence of bytes, not a string.  That has implications for how it is included in some formats, but as RFC 9651 limits its syntax to a pretty small subset of the ASCII range, this is mostly just a theoretical consideration, not a practical one.

* Parsing errors in RFC 9651 means that you lose everything.  No preference survives.  That means that authoring errors have consequences.  This is an artifact of the format being more of a computer-to-computer language, rather than being tolerant of human error.  I'm not thrilled with this, but recognize the trade-off involved.

* Repeated keys mean that only the last one is taken.  Again, not thrilled with this, but think that the trade is tolerable.

* Labels are lowercase only.  A lot of the list traffic has started to use "AI=whatever"; RFC 9651 doesn't let us shout.  I think that this is fine, but it's another minor ding.

* Some patterns of use that might be natural are invalid.  For instance, spaces around the "=" is invalid, so "ai = n" would result in a parsing error and no preference being registered.

Closes #8.

pulls.title: Removed reference to origin of TDM definition
pulls.author: paul2keller
pulls.body:
This pull request proposes to leave the definition of TDM unchanged, but removes the explicit reference that this is based on EU law. This is part based on a review of existing legal definitions of TDM in other jurisdictions that have TDM exceptions in ether copyright law: 

The UK does not have a proper definition in the law itself, but the UK government provides on as part of its Guidance on Exceptions to copyright which is very similar to the EU definition: 

"Text and data mining is the use of automated analytical techniques to analyse text and data for patterns, trends and other useful information."

The other two jurisdictions with TDM exceptions that I am aware of (Singapore and Japan) do not use the term TDM. Instead they anchor the exceptions on “computational data analysis” (SG) or “data analysis (JP). 

Given this it seems sensible to keep the definition of TDM as unchanged.

comments.author: paul2keller
comments.body:
Background and links to the relevant passages the copyright legislation of the above mentioned jurisdictions: 

### 🇪🇺 European Union:

In the EU the definition is laid down [in Article 2(2) of the Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/790/oj/eng#art_2):

> ‘text and data mining’ means any automated analytical technique aimed at analysing text and data in digital form in order to generate information which includes but is not limited to patterns, trends and correlations.
> 

### 🇬🇧 United Kingdom

The UK does not have a proper defintion in the law, but the UK government provides on as part of its [Guidance on Exceptions to copyright](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/exceptions-to-copyright):

> Text and data mining is the use of automated analytical techniques to analyse text and data for patterns, trends and other useful information.
> 

The [actual TDM exception in UK law](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1988/48/section/29A) specifies that it is not an infringement of copyright to "carry out a computational analysis of anything recorded in the work”

### 🇸🇬 Singapore (computational data analysis)

Singapore does not have a definition of TDM instead it defines the equivalent term “Computational data analysis” [in section 244 of its copyright code](https://sso.agc.gov.sg/Act/P15-P28-):

> “computational data analysis”, in relation to a work or a recording of a protected performance, includes 
(a)	using a computer program to identify, extract and analyse information or data from the work or recording; and
(b)	using the work or recording as an example of a type of information or data to improve the functioning of a computer program in relation to that type of information or data.
> 

### 🇯🇵 Japan (data analysis)

Japan does not have an explicit definition. [Here is the relevant text in Article 30-4](https://www.cric.or.jp/english/clj/cl2.html) is referred to as the Japanese TDM exception (emphasis mine):

> It is permissible to exploit a work, in any way and to the extent considered necessary, in any of the following cases, or in any other case in which it is not a person's purpose to personally enjoy or cause another person to enjoy the thoughts or sentiments expressed in that work; provided, however, that this does not apply if the action would unreasonably prejudice the interests of the copyright owner in light of the nature or purpose of the work or the circumstances of its exploitation:
> 
> 
> (i)　if it is done for use in testing to develop or put into practical use technology that is connected with the recording of sounds or visuals of a work or other such exploitation;
> 
> (ii)　**if it is done for use in data analysis (meaning the extraction, comparison, classification, or other statistical analysis of the constituent language, sounds, images, or other elemental data from a large number of works or a large volume of other such data**; the same applies in Article 47-5, paragraph (1), item (ii));

pulls.title: Add a description of how the model is interrogated
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
This is stacked on top of #26.  It just shows the incremental change.  (If it is accepted and #26 is not, we'll lose it.  Be careful.)

Rather than describe how defaults apply as part of the processing algorithm, I've made that part of how the model is consulted.  This doesn't have any functional impact in this case; the result is the same either way.

The main decision this makes is about the order in which things apply:

1. within a single statement, the most-specific statement applies (i.e., `genai` overrides `ai`)
2. across multiple statements, the least-permissive statement of preference applies (i.e., `n` overrides `y`)

We'll need to discuss which model we want to follow and be deliberate about it.

An example should help.  Consider two statements of preference that include no preference for nested categories: `ai=n` and `genai=y`.

In the proposed approach, the more general answer from the first statement fills in an answer for the `genai` category.  That's the model that this change adopts.  The final, combined answer for `genai` is determined by the `ai=n` preference because the value from that statement is taken first and a disallow preference overrides an allow preference (absent other information; see the text).

In an alternative model, preferences could be combined before resolving any inherited preferences.  That is, items 1 and 2 above are swapped to:

1. across multiple statements, the least permissive statement of preference for each category is selected
2. then any category without an assigned preference inherits the preference of any less-specific category

In that case, we'd be saying that `ai=n` leaves `genai` unspecified deliberately to allow another preference to set `genai=y` if they prefer.  Only if no other entity expresses a preference, does the implied `genai=n` apply.  In that model, we'd be assuming that the entity that sets `ai=n` knows about `genai` and chooses to defer to others on what the preference is.

I personally dislike the alternative.  It makes any vocabulary extension fraught with issues.  Consider that an extension we define later might carve out space for a new specialized usage (like `inference`, if we were to define that in three years time, or `commercial` or anything else we might defer).  That would put an unexpected hole in any established preference.  Anyone who previously said no to a class of usage could have that preference overridden for that specialized usage.

Structuring the document this way allows us to make a decision between these a little more easily than if the "processing" in #26 filled in values for `genai` from the value of `ai`.

Finally, the last decision in the change is that attachment mechanisms can define that one statement can override another.

That opens the possibility of us choosing to have the HTTP header override robots.txt or even having content metadata override any other preferences.  If we find that this isn't needed, that's fine, but I understand that this is still on the table.  Including it cost me little effort; removing it would be equally easy.

Using Specification Required gives some flexibility for the process to recognize emerging labels without a lot of procedural overhead, but it seems like this is angling toward IETF Review as the operative policy. pulls.title: A reframing of search
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
As discussed on the list recently.

This does not include Brad's suggestion of "for the exclusive purpose of".  That is an important clarification, but I think we need to address that separately.  That is, we need to recognize that what we conceive of as "search" applications are more complicated than a simple index that is used to locate stuff.  We need commentary that explains that a single application can embody multiple usage categories and that use of assets for each of those aspects can have separate rules.  This isn't necessarily how those applications are built today[^1], but that's not necessarily a constraint on what we do.

[^1]: I am reminded of the concept of a "data lake", which has no distinction about where data has come from, the purpose for which it was obtained, or anything along those lines, making compliance with data protection regulation impossible.  The analogy here is with respect to use of assets for multiple purposes, without distinction.  For data lakes, the introduction of things like GDPR helped application developers build discipline about how they obtain and label personal information; perhaps this requires a similar shift, albeit one that affects a smaller set of people.

pulls.title: robots.txt attachment: make path segment mandatory
pulls.author: bnewbold
pulls.body:
This updates the draft text to make the path segment mandatory instead of optional. The motivation is to make the `Content-Usage` directive read more clearly like the `Allow`/`Disallow` directives, and generally make robots.txt files more legible and understandable to humans (whether they have prior experience with robots.txt or not). This should have almost no impact on actual behavior or what preferences can be expressed. The trade-off is that every line will have two additional bytes for the case of "all paths", and that seems like a reasonable trade off for legibility.

A secondary benefit is that implementation becomes marginally easier: code will know there is always a leading path segment. While optional fields are common in protocols, it is more common to have trailing fields be optional, not leading fields. The current text *is* unambiguous about how to detect whether there is a path segment or not (if there is a leading `/` character), but this makes things just a bit easier to implement correctly.

I think this would be an improvement on the syntax and it would be great to get it in. However, I do want to prioritize moving work forward, and think this improvement is not worth holding things up.

comments.author: bnewbold
comments.body: To expand on thinking of this a bit more: I suspect if the path is optional, it will be common to not include it, and set overall preferences for entire websites, perhaps by group (eg, by named crawler). If that is a common pattern, it is possible for developers, hosts, and crawlers to never encounter a line with a path segment, and make incorrect assumptions about allowed syntax.

pulls.title: AI Output and Search categories
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
This is the output of the informali, impromptu design team that was formed during the last day of meetings.  This attempts to synthesize ideas from numerous sources, including various email threads on the mailing list, drafts shared (in particular
draft-madhavan-aipref-displaybasedpref) and some ideas that were floating around.

This concentrates on system outputs and aims to primarily address concerns about substitutive use.  That is, the potential for AI to generate content that is different from source material, but which might replace it.

We did not include some of the concepts that were in draft-madhavan-aipref-displaybasedpref about limiting output size and so forth, but recognize that those might make good extensions at a later time.  Those will depend on specific formats (text lengths for text, snippet duration for audio or video, etc..) and we concluded that we want to concentrate on the core concept.

This is a less flexible version of the thing that was presented.  Rather than having separate conditions of use attached to a permission grant, one for linking back and another for requiring direct quoting rather than paraphrasing or summarizing.  These too might need further refinement in future.  For example, we talked about how certain formats might be able to identify which content (text, time, whatever) is OK to quote and which is not.

This does not attempt to address the new problem this raises, which is that indicating that you would like these new categories to be allowed in practice also means that you need to say the same for AI training. That's not a problem this is attempting to solve.  We'll need to do that in some other way.

pulls.title: Switch training to foundation model production
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
This takes the two pre-existing model training categories and changes it into a foundation model training category.

There are a few challenges in our current definitions, particularly around the base "AI Training" category.  As some have noted, the definition of AI is a bit fuzzy.  This avoids that by relying on what is now a widely-recognized definition.

That definition is not uniform, so I'm following the sage advice of a colleague.  They suggested that making a definition for the specific use case is best, because it allows for the definition to fit better to the domain in which it is applied.

Some notes about aspects of "foundation model"
where this varies from accepted definitions:

* Some definitions make a point of including a measure of model size. US legislation says "tens of billions of parameters"; others suggest a firmer one billion parameter threshold.  Here, most definitions don't bother, except to note that the model is "large" and trained on lots of data.  Not being concrete seems like it will be safest.
* Many definitions refer to self-supervised learning as being typical in the creation of foundation models.  Because this is phrased with a "generally" or "typically" -- and because techniques can and do change -- it seemed like this wasn't a useful addition to the definition.
* This includes a note that the model has some generative capability. In direct contradiction to my previous note about "typically", that's a word I've used here.  My sense is that it is important to recognize this capability, particular as we are replacing the "generative AI training" category here.

The definition here includes fine-tuning.  This is not strictly a foundation model thing, but my view is that a fine-tuned model is highly likely to also be a foundation model.  Not including that in the definition would not be consistent with the spirit of the preferences. I acknowledge that this creates new questions and challenges -- what about techniques like LoRA? does the name really match the scope? -- but my view is that this is a better fit for expectations.

This does not remove any of the more general definitions that were created to support the previous definitions (AI, training, ML, etc...). My current view is that these are less critical now that the definition is essentially self-contained.  We might consider removing them later. They are certainly far less load-bearing now, so that is an easier decision to make.  (I'm coming to the view that each category should have a self-contained definition without relying on external definitions, so that puts those definitions on notice.)

pulls.title: Conformance -> understanding
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
This change attempts to reframe Sections 3.1 and 3.2 in terms of the two things they are intended to address, each separately.

* Section 3.1 is about what it means to understand what a preference is.

* Section 3.2 is about what it might mean to act on that understanding.

It seems like this distinction was unclear in the past and this is primarily an attempt to address that confusion.

At the risk of adding to the confusion though, I felt like it was responsible to talk about the limitations of what we can achieve in that first item.  After all, the system we describe has limitations.  Those are twofold:

1.  People who receive/obtain assets will not understand every possible way of expressing preferences.  So only those preferences they know about and choose to implement will be understood by them.

2.  We are not always offering a way to convey *who* expressed a preference.  Some mechanisms might depend on that (the registry ideas need to, for instance), but the ones we are defining today cannot.

Neither should be especially surprising to anyone, but writing something that is precise turned out to be tricky.  I'm not happy with where it is, but am turning to wider review for feedback.

If our intent is to capture the technical limitation — that understanding is bounded by what a recipient has implemented — something like "A recipient can only understand preferences expressed through mechanisms it has implemented" would be more precise and wouldn't risk being read as a general invitation to disregard preferences.

comments.author: tymrtn
comments.body:
Nice iteration on Leah's text. 

A few suggested changes, with rationale, followed by a fully incorporated version:

Suggested changes:

- Broaden the opening definition to plural: "to direct users to the locations of those assets". The singular "location of the asset" could be read to exclude multi-result search pages where users survey several options rather than being directed to one.

- Tighten model exclusivity constraint: "exclusively by the search application and exclusively for purposes of search as defined in this category". The current "used exclusively by the search application" is necessary but not sufficient; a model could be used by the search app for non-search purposes. Double-locking to both the application and the purpose closes that gap.

- Remove the "evaluating an asset" sentence: "That is, evaluating an asset for potential use is included" is orphaned from its antecedent and could open a loophole where any amount of processing is characterized as "evaluation." Better tracked as a separate issue.

- Broaden the summary exclusion back toward Leah's original: "summaries or other new content beyond verbatim excerpts or snippets". Naming only "summaries" invites recharacterization ("it's a synthesis, not a summary"). The broader phrasing from Leah's proposal in #173 is more defensive.

- Restore "verbatim": The old text required excerpts "drawn verbatim," which this iteration dropped. Without it, "snippets", a term commonly used for AI-generated preview text, could be read to permit generative output, undermining the core goal.

- Add a substitution test: Chris's original proposal in #173 included the principle that search should not "generate outputs which materially reduce the need to access the original asset." Framing this as a substitution test aligns with established copyright concepts (market substitution under the fourth fair use factor) and captures the underlying policy goal more directly than any specific list of prohibited output types.

Fully incorporated version:

```

## Search {#search}

The use of one or more assets in a search application to direct users to the locations of those assets.

This category of use has the following conditions:

* The presentation of an asset in search output  must include a direct reference or link to the original location from which the asset was retrieved.

* To assist users in evaluating the relevance of a result,  verbatim excerpts or snippets may be displayed  from the source asset.

The internal processing of assets to perform tasks such as indexing, ranking, and retrieval may involve the use and training of AI/ML models, provided that those models are used exclusively by the search application and exclusively for purposes of search as defined in this category. 

This category does not include the use of assets to generate summaries or other new content beyond verbatim excerpts or snippets as described above. More generally, this category does not include uses that generate outputs which serve as a substitute for the original asset.

```

pulls.title: Refine section 4.1 based on Toronto discussion
pulls.author: kelleyk
pulls.body:
Here are the proposed tweaks to the definition of model training that I mentioned on the interim call.  (This was originally homework from Toronto; sorry that it's taken so long to post.)  I think that this gets us to a description of what it means to train a general-purpose foundation model without relying on any of the words that have raised objections in past drafts.

The most substantive change I'm proposing in this PR is that we move from talking about a model that "can generate" to one that "is used, or made available for use, to generate."  One of the things that I heard most clearly in Toronto from people thinking about declaring preferences was concern about the subjectivity of definitions based on purpose and intent, and about the possibility that either might change over time.

This makes the category slightly more narrow, but also more objective—something either was used or it wasn't; much less is subject to interpretation.  The same property should let implementers apply the category consistently, too.

This approach also focuses on the activity rather than the technology, which I hope addresses the concerns that were raised in Toronto about unintended consequences.

I've expanded "used" to "used, or made available for use" in an attempt to address the concerns that were raised about open-weight models and organizational boundaries.

I've replaced the "produce or refine" language in the current draft with "modify", which I think encompasses both; producing a model is the process of iteratively refining its weights.

I've also kept "asset" from the current draft.  I know that some folks had concerns about that term in Toronto; I don't feel strongly about it, so long as we have a word for "piece of data".

comments.author: B1ueD0g
comments.body:
A small framing point from the list discussion: I think it helps to keep two questions separate here:

1. the vocabulary category: whether the asset is used to modify model state that can later be used to generate content; and
2. the propagation/attachment question: whether preference information has to travel with a dataset or model artifact so a downstream actor can evaluate it.

For this PR, I would keep section 4.1 mostly on the first question. The open-weight case is important, but if "made available for use" carries too much weight, it can start to sound like model publication itself triggers the preference even where the downstream actor does not have enough attached context to evaluate it.

One possible direction would be something like:

> Using an asset to modify an AI model that is used, or made available for use by another actor, to generate content in one or more modalities.

Then, if useful, a short note could say that passing preference information with datasets or model artifacts is a processing/metadata question, not something this vocabulary definition by itself specifies.

That keeps the definition objective, while not forcing this PR to resolve the larger chain-of-custody question.
