pulls.title: Add "AI System Inference" and "AI User Input" categories
pulls.author: natehake
pulls.body:
This adds two proposed inference/use vocab categories that are intended to work in tandem: 
-AI System Inference 
-AI User Input

These definitions both rely on the AI training definition of PR 211 as a logical starting point. They define inference as all use of assets by AI models beyond the modification of learned parameters. 

Together, these proposed categories would enable the expression of preferences covering the full field of post-training usage. They also give declaring parties the option to express different preferences when assets are used by autonomous systems vs when assets are identified by a human end user.

comments.author: sposth
comments.body:
I like the distinction between system-selected and user-selected assets, but I think the definitions can be much clearer.

The key distinction is not inference itself, but who identifies the asset used during inference.

For example:

**AI System Inference**

Using an asset during inference by an AI system where the asset is identified or retrieved by the system itself. Inference means all use beyond the modification of an AI model's learned parameters.

**AI User Input**

Using an asset during inference by an AI system where the asset has been explicitly identified by a human user. This includes assets provided directly by the user or assets whose location has been explicitly specified by the user. Inference means all use beyond the modification of an AI model's learned parameters.

This makes the distinction immediately visible:

- the system selects or retrieves the asset; or
- the human explicitly selects the asset.

The rest of the definition is common to both categories.

I also think another aspect deserves discussion.

The phrase

> "by providing either the asset itself or a location from which it can be retrieved"

does more than define the category. It also implies different attachment and discovery mechanisms.

A directly provided asset can carry an attached preference signal, for example through embedded metadata, a sidecar file, or an associated registry declaration. By contrast, when a user provides a URL or domain, the preference is most likely resolved through a location-based mechanism rather than being attached directly to the asset.

It would therefore be useful to clarify whether these are simply equivalent ways of identifying an asset, or whether the specification expects different attachment and discovery mechanisms depending on whether the user provides the asset itself or only a reference to its location. If the latter is intended, making this explicit may be worthwhile, as it has implications for implementers.

One additional observation concerns the naming. The distinction is really about who selected the asset, not about the inference process itself. For that reason, names such as **System-selected Assets** and **User-selected Assets**, or **System-selected Inference** and **User-directed Inference**, may communicate the distinction more clearly than AI User Input, which could easily be interpreted as referring to prompts rather than to the source material used during inference.

comments.author: coopdanger
comments.body:
1. When using the word "beyond" in the phrase "beyond the modification of an AI model's learned parameters," does "beyond" mean "after" or does "beyond" mean "except"? 

2. I think the term "inference" should be defined in Section 2 rather than here, which would allow "Inference means all use beyond the modification of an AI model's learned parameters" to be removed from this section.

3. I think Sebastian's suggested re-labeling of these two categories is useful but it might be clearer if they were symmetric: **system-directed inference** and **user-directed inference**. 

4. I think the interactions between system-directed inference and the search category will require a lot of clarification. If an expressed preference says "search=y;system-inference=n," how is that supposed to be interpreted by a search application?

pulls.title: Add Selection Step, Inference User, Inference System
pulls.author: tymrtn
pulls.body:
This refines #216 by defining the boundary between user-directed and system-directed inference. Nate's original commits are preserved at the base; this rebases onto -07 and adds two things.

First, a "selection step" that makes the user/system distinction mechanical: an operation by any party or process other than the user that identifies assets in response to a request (searching, browsing, ranking, recommending, resolving a description). Retrieval from among assets the user previously provided is not a selection step.

Second, the two category definitions rewritten around that term. User-directed: the user provided the asset or a direct reference the system fetches without any selection step. System-directed: everything else, including further assets fetched of the system's own choosing. Applies at time of use regardless of acquisition.

Under §6.4, categories not in the base document degrade to "unknown" permanently for conforming recipients. If inference categories are going in, they need to be here before this ships.

A decision-tree tool that walks scenarios through the vocabulary is at 
[The Inference Line](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/a4a1f206-1759-454b-8b03-90861d8d110b)

Addresses discussion in #216 from @natehake, @paul2keller, @ekr, @martinthomson, @TimidRobot, @chrisn, @lrosenthol, and @posth.

We've agreed not to have overlap between categories, but this creates an overlap with the infer-user category.

It also potentially overlaps with search, which is a problem with @natehake's original as well.  A specific exclusion, in one or other direction, could address that.  That is, you could say that if search applies, then either inference category does not apply.  I'd make a change to the search definition in that case.

(I don't think that the opposite makes a lot of sense, because search is a more specific scope than training or inference, even with the qualifications here.)

Infer-system's definition opens with "any other circumstance" — other than infer-user. So it can't overlap infer-user; it's built as everything infer-user doesn't cover. The one place I can see it leaking is the last sentence, if "regardless of when or how the asset was acquired" reads as an independent scope grant rather than timing detail inside the complement:

> Whether this category applies is determined at the time of use, according to how the asset was identified for that use rather than when it was acquired.

On search, can you help me understand the overlap you're seeing? [4.2 is about snippets and links to assets](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-07#section-4.2), not generating content, so it shouldn't clear the inference gate at all. datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-07#section-4.2 AI-generated search results overviews already route to inference by the summary exclusion in 4.2.

The general consensus is that search is always inference.

There's some contention, but search is sometimes training, which is why we explicitly allow training if it is exclusively for a search application.  The same would apply to inference.

I don't think that "any other" is sufficiently clear.

pulls.title: Remove text on presentation restrictions in search
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
Not remembering exactly why this text was added makes this hard. My theory is that the intent was to make it clear that restrictions on how assets are presented in search are made relative to the way in which the asset is presented: it's language and the format (text vs. voice vs. video, etc...) in particular.  In that way, it would make no sense to apply a transformation (text-to-speech, say) for accessibility reasons and only then try to apply a presentation restriction (100 character limit as an example of something that makes no sense).

However, that's not an us problem.  Anyone defining such a restriction - or anyone choosing to apply a transformation - can make a better decision about this than us.  Let us not burden our definitions, which are already fraught enough, with this additional wrinkle.

See discussion at https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ai-control/JKSRzKZ1_Dfkqpvh70-7irJm_ZA

comments.author: Farzaneh-Unicode
comments.body:
This is an excerpt from Krishna et al draft on search which I think can clarify the opt-out opt-in options in search: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-madhavan-aipref-displaybasedpref/  4.1.  Indexing and Retrieval

   The act of allowing or disallowing content collected by web crawlers
   from being indexed or retrieved for purposes of display.  Such
   preference mechanism can also be applied for cases where digital
   content is not accessible.  In existing implementations, access
   preferences are typically expressed via the NOINDEX statement set in
   HTTP header or meta tags.

4.2.  Display text

   The act of allowing or disallowing a reproduction of text content
   collected by a web crawler, except for the title if specified, from
   the whole or parts of the content to display portions of that
   content.  In existing implementations preference on which text can be
   used for caption are expressed via the NOSNIPPET statement set in
   http header, HTML meta tags, or HTML tags properties (data-
   nosnippet).

4.3.  Display text length

   The act of limiting the number of characters as a textual display
   from content collected by a web crawler.  In existing implementations
   quotation length preferences are expressed via the max-snippet
   statement set in http header or HTML robots meta tags.

4.4.  Exact text match

   The act of limiting text content to only an exact match if displaying
   text content from the document.  If this preference is present, text
   content must be quoted as is or use avoided and an explicit link back
   to the source of the document used in that instance.  One example of
   existing implementation of text quotation preferences is notranslate.



4.5.  Image preview

   The act of limiting usage and size of images.  In existing
   implementations image preview preferences are typically expressed via
   the max-image-preview statement set in http header or HTML meta tags.

4.6.  Video preview

   The act of limiting usage and length of videos.  In existing
   implementations video preview preferences are typically expressed via
   the max-video-preview statement set in http header or HTML robots
   meta tags.

pulls.title: Distinguish acquisition and use
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
Any system of preferences like what we have naturally has no guards on assets being acquired.  The preferences that declaring parties express only apply to how the asset is subsequently used.

This attempts to document that more clearly.  It also highlights the need to retain preferences along with assets if their use does not immediately follow acquisition (which is likely to be the typical case, with immediate use being the abnormal case).

This doesn't address #246, but it creates a place where that might be more naturally addressed, by saying that intermediate forms or transformations of assets (such as embeddings created from assets) might also need to retain preferences if they might subsequently be used.

Closes #167.
Closes #193.
